keywords: saas, software, platform, app, tool, product, subscription, web app, cloud, service
visual_style: Clean and confident with restrained use of color. Prioritize whitespace and visual hierarchy over decoration. Typography should feel modern-professional - not startup-playful, not enterprise-heavy. Avoid gradients, rounded-everything, and illustration-heavy styles that date quickly. The interface should feel like a tool people trust with daily work: calm, structured, and visually quiet so content and data can breathe. Density should be medium - not as sparse as a marketing site, not as packed as a trading terminal.
landing_page: Hero section leads with the core value proposition in one sentence, not a feature list. Below the fold: three benefits (not features), each with a concrete outcome. Social proof section uses logos or a single compelling testimonial, not a wall of quotes. CTA is singular and high-contrast - never compete with secondary actions above the fold. Pricing section shows 2-3 tiers max with the recommended tier visually emphasized. Footer carries trust signals: security badges, compliance logos, support availability. Avoid: carousels, auto-playing videos, multiple competing CTAs, and hero images that say nothing about the product.
dashboard_layout: Left sidebar navigation with collapsible groups - keep top-level items concise and grouped logically. Main content area uses a 12-column grid with card-based sections for key metrics at the top. Tables and lists dominate the content area with consistent sort, filter, and search patterns. Right panel or modal for detail views - avoid full-page navigations that break context. Breadcrumbs for nested views. Status indicators use semantic colors consistently (green/amber/red). Empty states are helpful, not decorative - tell users what to do, not just that nothing is here. Avoid: tab overload, deeply nested navigation, dashboard widgets users cannot customize or dismiss.
color_palette: Use a single primary brand color at 10-15% surface coverage - it should anchor the interface without overwhelming it. CTAs get the highest-saturation variant of the primary or a complementary accent; everything else stays neutral. Background is near-white or very light gray, never pure white (too clinical) or tinted (dates fast). Text is near-black on light backgrounds with at least 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Semantic colors are reserved strictly for meaning: green for success, amber for warnings, red for errors and destructive actions - never use these as decorative accents. Dark mode inverts the luminance scale but keeps the same hue relationships; do not introduce new colors in dark mode. Avoid: using brand color for large background fills, rainbow status systems, low-contrast placeholder text, or gray-on-gray interactive elements.
essential_ux: Every action that modifies data needs a clear undo path or confirmation step - especially delete, bulk operations, and settings changes. Provide feedback for any operation exceeding 100ms - use skeleton screens for content areas, spinners only for discrete actions. Error messages appear inline next to the field that caused them, not in toast notifications that disappear before users read them. Forms should use a hybrid validation approach: validate format constraints on blur, validate complex rules on submit with an error summary linking to each field. Never clear a form after a validation error. Session timeout must warn before expiring and preserve unsaved work. Navigation should never lose unsaved changes without warning. Search must be forgiving: handle typos, partial matches, and return useful empty states. Keyboard shortcuts for power users, but never as the only path to an action. Onboarding should be progressive - reveal complexity as users demonstrate readiness, not in an upfront tutorial users will skip. Avoid: modals on top of modals, disabled buttons without explanation, pagination when infinite scroll fits, and confirmation dialogs for non-destructive actions.
ui_style_bias: Structured, professional, and calm UI; emphasizes whitespace, card grids, and restrained color. Focus on clarity and confidence over flair.

Typography should be readable and neutral, leaning friendly but never playful. Visual hierarchy must be obvious at a glance. Avoid complex visual systems, decorative motion, gradients, or brand-heavy styling that suggests scale or process overhead the product does not have.
landing_page: The hero must immediately answer three questions: what this does, who it is for, and what problem it replaces. Use a concrete example or screenshot, not abstract messaging. Below the fold: a short 'how it works' section (3 steps max), followed directly by pricing. Pricing must be visible without interaction. Social proof should be lightweight but credible (usage counts, indie testimonials, integrations). Use a single primary CTA focused on immediate use, not commitment. Avoid: long narratives, hidden pricing, multiple personas, or sales-oriented language.
dashboard_layout: Many Micro SaaS products should not start with a dashboard. Default entry point should be the core workflow or output. Navigation must be shallow and obvious - ideally 3-5 primary destinations. Favor single-column or simple two-column layouts. Defaults matter more than customization; preconfigure sensible states. Inline actions and immediate feedback are preferred over multi-step flows. Empty states must demonstrate value using examples or sample data. Avoid: settings-first experiences, feature toggles, permission models, or dashboards that require setup before usefulness.
color_palette: Use a neutral base with one accent color to guide attention. Brand color should be reserved for primary actions only. Backgrounds should be light and unobtrusive. Contrast must meet accessibility standards, but the system can be simpler than enterprise SaaS. Semantic colors should be limited to success, warning, and error states only. Dark mode is optional and should not be implemented unless user demand is clear. Avoid: loud palettes, over-branding, or color systems more complex than the product itself.
essential_ux: Time-to-value is the primary UX constraint. Users should reach a meaningful result within minutes. Anything that does not directly support the core use case should be deferred or removed. Onboarding should be implicit: sample data, defaults, and guided empty states outperform tutorials. Errors must be reversible and non-punitive. Performance issues are trust-breaking at this scale. Documentation should be short, searchable, and optional. Avoid: mandatory onboarding flows, configuration before value, hidden complexity, or UX patterns that assume team-based usage.
ui_style_bias: Simple, lightweight UI; emphasizes immediacy, clarity, and functional hierarchy. Minimalist components, single accent color, and fast entry points for core workflows.

essential_ux: Accuracy, transparency, and comprehension are critical. Provide immediate feedback for data input, updates, and errors. Ensure all metrics have clear context and definitions. Avoid ambiguous reporting, hidden assumptions, or misleading visualizations.
ui_style_bias: Clean, data-centric UI; emphasizes transparency, clarity, and actionable ESG insights

keywords: remote, collaboration, teamwork, project, chat, task, productivity, workspace
visual_style: Functional, efficient, and context-aware. Prioritize visibility of tasks, communications, and project states. Avoid clutter or hidden interactions that block workflows.
landing_page: Landing page must immediately convey platform capabilities: task tracking, communication, document sharing. Include clear examples of workflows. Single high-contrast CTA to sign up or demo. Avoid marketing fluff or hidden key actions.
dashboard_layout: Dashboard emphasizes projects, tasks, team activity, and deadlines. Filters, search, and notifications always visible. Collaboration tools (chat, file sharing) easily accessible. Avoid buried settings or confusing multi-step flows.
color_palette: Neutral base with accent colors highlighting priority tasks, notifications, or deadlines. Semantic colors only for state feedback. Avoid decorative palettes that interfere with focus or readability.
essential_ux: Collaboration must be frictionless. Provide inline guidance, status updates, and undo options. Ensure mobile and accessibility support. Avoid lost context, hidden notifications, or non-intuitive workflows.
ui_style_bias: Efficient, productivity-first UI; emphasizes clarity, task visibility, and minimal friction in team workflows

keywords: event, ticket, management, booking, registration, attendee, venue, schedule, tickets
visual_style: Organized, clear, and trust-inspiring. Prioritize discoverability of events, seating, and purchase options. Avoid confusing flows or excessive decorative elements.
landing_page: Landing page showcases upcoming events, highlights key info (date, location, availability), and provides a clear purchase path. Include social proof or reviews selectively. Single primary CTA to register or buy. Avoid hidden pricing or crowded messaging.
dashboard_layout: Dashboard foregrounds events, attendees, bookings, and analytics. Filters, search, and sorting clearly labeled. Provide real-time updates on sales and availability. Avoid deeply nested menus or unclear actions.
color_palette: Neutral background with brand accent highlighting CTAs and availability. Semantic colors for status indicators (available, sold out, pending). Avoid overly decorative palettes competing with content.
essential_ux: Transaction clarity and trust are paramount. Confirm bookings, show pricing clearly, provide receipts and confirmations. Avoid multi-step surprises, hidden fees, or confusing ticket allocations.
ui_style_bias: Trustworthy, organized UI; emphasizes event clarity, booking confidence, and actionable CTAs

keywords: mental health, therapy, wellness, mindfulness, meditation, counseling, self-care, mood, journal
visual_style: Calm, accessible, and emotionally safe. Use soft color palettes, generous whitespace, and rounded shapes that reduce visual tension. Typography must be highly legible with warm, humanistic typefaces — avoid clinical or cold sans-serifs. Every visual choice should lower cognitive load and create a sense of safety. Avoid neumorphism (poor contrast and accessibility), harsh edges, aggressive animations, or dark patterns that create urgency or guilt.
landing_page: Landing page must lead with emotional safety and privacy assurance — not feature lists. Communicate what the app helps with, who it is for, and how privacy is protected, all above the fold. Below the fold: a simple 3-step how-it-works, followed by credentialed endorsements (licensed therapists, clinical partnerships). Always include a visible crisis resource link (988 Lifeline or equivalent) in the footer and on key screens. Single CTA focused on low-commitment entry (explore, try free). Avoid: testimonials that feel exploitative, before/after framing, urgency tactics, or requiring account creation before showing value.
dashboard_layout: Navigation must be shallow (3-5 items) with clear, non-clinical labels (e.g., "Journal" not "CBT Module"). Default view should be the primary therapeutic tool (mood tracker, journal, meditation) — not a dashboard of metrics. Progress visualizations must frame setbacks as normal, never punitive — use streak-free designs or forgiving streak models that celebrate return, not shame absence. Session history and mood data should be private by default with explicit opt-in for sharing. Provide offline access for core features. Avoid: gamification that creates guilt, leaderboards, social comparison, or data-dense dashboards that medicalize the experience.
color_palette: Soft, muted palette grounded in calming tones — pale blues, sage greens, warm lavenders, soft peach. Background should be warm off-white, never stark white or dark. Primary accent used sparingly for positive actions only. Avoid red for any non-critical purpose — use warm amber for gentle alerts. Semantic colors must be softened: muted green for progress, gentle amber for check-ins. Never use high-saturation or vibrant colors that create arousal or anxiety. Dark mode should use warm dark tones (dark blue-gray, not pure black) to maintain the calming atmosphere.
essential_ux: Emotional safety is the primary UX constraint. Users may be in crisis, distressed, or cognitively impaired — design for the worst emotional state, not the best. All destructive actions (deleting journal entries, ending sessions) must have clear undo paths. Never auto-delete user emotional data. Session interruptions must save state automatically. Crisis resources must be accessible from any screen within one tap — never behind menus or modals. Mood tracking inputs should offer a spectrum, not binary good/bad choices. Notifications must be gentle and opt-in, never guilt-inducing ("You haven't logged in 3 days"). Privacy indicators must be visible on every screen that handles sensitive data. Onboarding should be warm and gradual, asking only what is needed for the first session. Support screen readers, scalable text, and reduced-motion preferences. Avoid: streaks that punish breaks, pop-up modals during emotional exercises, social features that expose mental health status, or any dark pattern that leverages vulnerability.
ui_style_bias: Calm, accessible UI with soft shapes, warm tones, and emotionally safe interactions

keywords: pet, pets, animal, veterinary, vet, dog, cat, tracker, pet health
visual_style: Warm, friendly, and approachable with playful personality that avoids being childish. Use rounded shapes, soft shadows, and cheerful micro-interactions. Typography should feel friendly and readable — rounded sans-serifs work well. Visual hierarchy must clearly separate pet profiles, health data, and action items. Avoid clinical aesthetics that feel like a veterinary chart or overly cutesy designs that undermine trust for health features.
landing_page: Landing page should showcase a pet profile with key features (health tracking, reminders, social). Lead with the emotional bond — pet owners care about their pet's wellbeing, not feature specs. Include a clear visual of the core experience (pet profile card, health timeline). Below the fold: 3 key benefits with pet-centric imagery, followed by vet partnership badges or user testimonials. Single CTA to add your first pet. Avoid: stock photos of generic pets, feature-heavy hero sections, or aggressive subscription pushes before demonstrating value.
dashboard_layout: Pet profile is the hub — all navigation radiates from the individual pet. Multi-pet households need easy switching (tab bar or avatar row, not dropdown). Health dashboard shows upcoming vaccinations, medications, weight trends, and vet visits in a timeline view. Activity and feeding logs should support quick-entry patterns (one-tap logging). Photo gallery integrated into the profile, not siloed. Reminders and alerts for vaccinations, medications, and appointments must be prominent but not alarming. Avoid: dashboards that require setup before showing value, complex multi-step flows for daily logging, or hiding health records behind multiple taps.
color_palette: Warm, earthy base with playful accent colors — soft oranges, warm greens, sky blues. Background warm off-white or cream. Species-specific accent themes are a nice touch but optional. Semantic colors: green for healthy/up-to-date, amber for upcoming/due soon, red only for overdue or urgent. Photo backgrounds should have subtle overlays to maintain text readability. Avoid: clinical blues that feel like a vet clinic, neon or high-saturation palettes, or dark themes that diminish the warm, friendly feel.
essential_ux: Pet data entry must be fast and forgiving — owners log meals, walks, and symptoms daily, so one-tap or minimal-tap entry is critical. Vaccination and medication reminders must support snooze and reschedule, not just dismiss. Health records should be exportable or shareable with veterinarians (PDF or direct integration). Photo upload must handle the reality of pet photography — motion blur, poor lighting, multiple attempts. Weight and health trend charts should use clear, non-alarming visualization with context (breed-normal ranges where available). Multi-pet support must not create data silos — household-level views for shared appointments or expenses. Offline access for basic pet profile and health records. Avoid: requiring breed selection from an exhaustive list (offer search + common breeds first), hiding emergency vet info, or social features that share pet health data without explicit consent.
ui_style_bias: Warm, playful UI with pet-centric profiles, quick-entry logging, and cheerful micro-interactions

keywords: smart home, iot, home automation, device, sensor, connected, hub, automation
visual_style: Dark-mode-first with high-contrast status indicators. Layout must prioritize at-a-glance device status and quick control access. Typography should be clean, medium-weight, and legible at small sizes for dense device grids. Use consistent iconography for device types and states. Avoid decorative elements that compete with real-time status information or slow down interaction with controls.
landing_page: Landing page must demonstrate the control experience — show a realistic dashboard mockup or interactive demo, not abstract smart home illustrations. Communicate supported device ecosystems and setup simplicity. Below the fold: integration list (Google, Alexa, HomeKit, Matter), security/privacy assurances, and setup timeline expectation. Single CTA to start setup or explore compatible devices. Avoid: futuristic renders that misrepresent the actual UI, hidden compatibility lists, or feature dumps without context.
dashboard_layout: Room-based or zone-based primary navigation with a global overview home screen showing all device statuses at a glance. Quick-action controls (toggle lights, adjust thermostat, lock doors) must be accessible within one tap from the home screen. Device cards show current state, last-updated timestamp, and battery/connectivity status. Automation rules should be visible and editable inline — not buried in settings. Energy monitoring surfaces daily/weekly trends with cost estimation. Alert history and device health accessible but not dominating the primary view. Avoid: flat device lists without spatial grouping, controls that require navigating to a device detail page for simple on/off actions, or automation builders that require programming knowledge.
color_palette: Dark mode default with near-black backgrounds (#1a1a2e or similar). Status indicator colors must be consistent and unambiguous: green for active/online, amber for warning/low battery, red for offline/error, blue for standby/cooling. White or light gray text with high contrast. Accent color for primary interactive controls (buttons, sliders, toggles). Room or zone headers can use subtle color differentiation. Light mode alternative should maintain the same semantic color meanings. Avoid: colored backgrounds per room that fragment the visual system, or dim/subtle status indicators that are hard to scan at a glance.
essential_ux: Reliability and immediacy are paramount — users depend on this for home safety (locks, alarms, cameras). Control feedback must be instantaneous; if a command is in-flight, show a pending state, never an ambiguous toggle. Device offline states must be clearly communicated with last-known-good values shown. Automation failures must notify proactively, not silently fail. Support graceful degradation when internet is down — local control for critical devices. Accessibility: controls must be operable via keyboard, voice, and screen readers. Provide clear labeling for all icons. Battery and connectivity warnings should appear before devices go offline. Scene/routine activation needs confirmation for security-sensitive actions (unlock door, disable alarm). Avoid: silent failures, ambiguous device states, controls that require precision targeting on small touch areas, or notifications that cannot distinguish routine events from genuine alerts.
ui_style_bias: Dark, status-driven UI; emphasizes real-time device control, room-based navigation, and high-contrast indicators

keywords: ev, electric vehicle, charging, charging station, range, battery, energy
visual_style: Clean, modern, and data-forward with an environmental undertone. Prioritize map-based discovery, real-time availability, and clear numerical displays for range, cost, and charge times. Typography should be clean and slightly technical — good at rendering numbers, units, and measurements. Use spacious layouts that accommodate map views alongside data panels. Avoid cluttered interfaces or purely decorative green-washing visuals.
landing_page: Landing page must immediately show value: find a charger, estimate range, or calculate costs. Include an interactive map preview or location search above the fold. Below the fold: supported charger networks, vehicle compatibility, pricing transparency, and environmental impact metrics (CO2 saved, kWh delivered). Single CTA to find nearest charger or plan a route. Trust signals: network partnerships, uptime statistics. Avoid: stock photos of EVs without functional UI context, hidden pricing, or vague environmental claims without data.
dashboard_layout: Map-centric primary view with list/filter sidebar. Charger pins show real-time availability (available, in-use, out-of-service, coming soon) with color coding. Detail panel for selected station: connector types, pricing, amenities, wait time estimation, and user ratings. Trip planner integrates range estimation with charging stops, showing time/cost per stop. Vehicle profile stores battery capacity, current charge, and connector type for personalized estimates. Charge session history with cost breakdown. Avoid: map views that require zooming to find chargers, hidden connector compatibility info, or trip planners that ignore real-time availability.
color_palette: Clean neutrals with electric blue (#009CD1 or similar) as primary accent and green as secondary for environmental/sustainability cues. Map pins use traffic-light convention: green (available), amber (limited/waitlist), red (offline/out-of-service), gray (unknown/coming soon). Background light and clean to support map readability. Data visualizations use the blue-green spectrum. Avoid: excessive green-washing (all-green palettes that reduce information density), dark themes that make maps hard to read in daylight, or low-contrast status indicators on map pins.
essential_ux: Range anxiety is the core user emotion to address. Always show remaining range alongside charging time estimates — never one without the other. Pricing must be transparent before charging begins: per-kWh cost, idle fees, session fees, and estimated total. Real-time availability must be genuinely real-time with clear timestamps. Trip planning must account for weather, elevation, and driving style impacts on range (or clearly state when estimates are idealized). Connector compatibility must be checked against the user's vehicle before recommending a station. Charge session status must be accessible remotely with push notifications for completion, interruption, or errors. Support offline access for recently viewed stations and saved routes. Avoid: optimistic range estimates that strand users, hidden idle fees, stations shown as available when data is stale, or requiring account creation before searching for chargers.
ui_style_bias: Clean, map-centric UI; emphasizes real-time availability, range confidence, and transparent pricing

keywords: subscription, box, curation, unboxing, monthly, quarterly, membership, personalize, recurring
visual_style: Vibrant, expressive, and anticipation-driven. Layouts should build excitement while maintaining clarity about what subscribers receive and when. Use bold imagery, playful motion for reveals, and modular content blocks. Typography should feel energetic but readable — slightly playful for marketing, neutral for account management. Avoid clinical or overly minimalist designs that drain the excitement from discovery and unboxing.
landing_page: Landing page must communicate the unboxing experience — use lifestyle photography or video of actual box contents, not abstract graphics. Lead with the curation promise (who selects, how personalization works). Below the fold: sample box contents with specific items shown, pricing tiers with clear comparison, and a personalization quiz preview. Social proof via unboxing videos, subscriber counts, or influencer features. Single CTA to take the quiz or subscribe. Gift options visible but secondary. Avoid: hiding box contents entirely (some preview builds trust), vague curation claims, or subscription terms buried in fine print.
dashboard_layout: Account dashboard foregrounds: next box date, shipment tracking, past boxes with item lists, and subscription management. Personalization preferences should be easily adjustable (quiz retake, preference toggles) without contacting support. Past box history should serve as a product catalog — link to full-size product purchases or reviews. Refer-a-friend and gift flows should be one-click accessible. Cancellation and pause flows must be straightforward (1-2 steps, no dark patterns like multi-page retention funnels). Avoid: hiding cancellation behind chat-only support, past boxes that disappear after delivery, or subscription management that requires desktop access.
color_palette: Vibrant brand palette with 2-3 energetic accent colors reflecting the box category (beauty: warm pinks and golds; food: rich oranges and greens; lifestyle: versatile blues and corals). Background light and clean to let product photography dominate. Seasonal palette variations are encouraged to match themed boxes. Semantic colors for subscription status: active (green), pausing (amber), expiring (red), gifted (gold or purple). Avoid: muted or corporate palettes that kill the excitement, dark themes that diminish product photography, or inconsistent palettes across marketing and account management.
essential_ux: Anticipation and trust are the dual UX drivers. Surprise elements (themed reveals, countdown timers to ship date) build engagement, but subscription terms, pricing, and cancellation must be completely transparent — no dark patterns. Personalization quiz should be short (5-7 questions max), visually engaging, and clearly explain how answers influence curation. Shipment tracking must be integrated, not just a carrier link. Product feedback on past items should influence future boxes — make this connection visible. Gift flows must handle different shipping addresses cleanly. Trial-to-paid conversions must be explicitly confirmed, never silent. Avoid: auto-renewal without clear reminders, skip/pause options hidden in settings, cancellation flows longer than 2 steps, or personalization that feels like it has no effect on actual box contents.
ui_style_bias: Vibrant, anticipation-driven UI; emphasizes discovery, personalization, and transparent subscription management

keywords: podcast, audio, episode, show, listen, stream, creator, rss
visual_style: Audio-first interface where the player is central and persistent. Dark mode default suits focused listening sessions. Layouts must balance discovery browsing with the always-present playback controls. Typography should be clean and scannable for episode lists and show notes. Use waveform or audio-related visual motifs sparingly as design accents, not decoration. Avoid video-centric design patterns that ignore audio's unique affordances.
landing_page: Landing page must communicate the listening experience — feature trending shows, curated playlists, and genre discovery. Include a playable sample or trending episode clip above the fold. Below the fold: creator tools overview (for dual-sided platforms), supported podcast apps/RSS, and content categories. For creator-focused platforms: emphasize analytics, monetization, and distribution. Single CTA to start listening or claim your show. Avoid: walls of podcast artwork with no context, auto-playing full episodes, or burying the search/discovery experience.
dashboard_layout: Persistent mini-player at bottom with expand-to-full capability — playback must never be interrupted by navigation. Episode lists show duration, publish date, and progress indicators for partially-played episodes. Queue management with drag-to-reorder. Playback speed control (0.5x-3x) and skip-silence feature accessible from the player, not settings. Show pages display episode list, show notes, and subscription status. Discovery via algorithmic recommendations, curated lists, and category browsing. For creator dashboards: episode analytics (downloads, completion rates, drop-off points), audience demographics, and monetization metrics. Avoid: players that restart episodes on navigation, episode lists without duration or progress, or discovery that only surfaces popular shows.
color_palette: Dark mode default with near-black or very dark gray background. Artwork colors can dynamically accent the player interface (extract dominant color from cover art) but must maintain text contrast — always test extracted colors against WCAG thresholds. Primary accent for play/subscribe actions. Waveform visualizations use the accent color. Episode progress bars clearly distinguish played, buffered, and remaining segments. Light mode alternative must maintain the same functional color system. Avoid: pure black backgrounds that make artwork float, dynamic colors that create unreadable text, or genre-specific color systems that confuse navigation.
essential_ux: Audio playback continuity is the primary UX constraint — never interrupt or restart playback due to navigation, errors, or app state changes. Download management for offline listening must be clear: show download progress, storage used, and auto-download preferences per show. Playback position sync across devices is expected. Chapter markers and timestamp links in show notes should seek the player accurately. Accessibility: provide transcripts where available, support screen readers for all player controls, and ensure playback controls are keyboard-navigable. Episode completion should auto-advance to next in queue. Avoid: players without variable speed, episode pages that lack show notes, search that only matches titles (not descriptions or transcripts), or creator analytics dashboards that show vanity metrics without actionable insights like listener drop-off points.
ui_style_bias: Dark, audio-focused UI; emphasizes persistent playback, episode progress, and waveform-accented design

keywords: dating, match, romance, relationship, swipe, profile, singles, love
visual_style: Warm, vibrant, and personality-forward. Interface must foreground photos and personal expression while maintaining safety and consent throughout. Use bold, warm colors and smooth animations for match interactions. Typography should feel modern and approachable — not corporate. Card-based layouts work naturally for profile browsing. Avoid clinical or transactional aesthetics that reduce people to data points.
landing_page: Landing page must lead with the platform's differentiator — what makes this dating experience unique (algorithm, community, niche). Show real-feeling profile examples (with consent or illustrated). Communicate safety features and verification process prominently. Below the fold: success stories (with consent), community size/quality indicators, and platform values. Single CTA for sign-up with clear expectation of what onboarding involves. Avoid: objectifying imagery, vague promises, hidden premium features, or onboarding that feels like a job application.
dashboard_layout: Profile cards are the core browsing unit — photo-first with name, age, and key compatibility signals visible without tapping. Swipe or explicit action buttons (like, pass, super-like) must be large, distinct, and unambiguous. Match screen provides clear next steps (message prompt, icebreaker suggestions). Conversation list shows unread status, last message preview, and match age. Discovery filters should balance specificity with pool size — warn when filters are too restrictive. Avoid: infinite scrolling through profiles without context (show compatibility reasons), hiding profile details behind multiple taps, match notifications that expire and create false urgency, or messaging interfaces that differ from standard chat patterns.
color_palette: Warm gradient palette — coral, rose, soft red, and warm amber as primary spectrum. Background warm white or very light warm gray. Accent colors for match celebrations and notifications. Profile cards should have neutral backgrounds that do not compete with user photos. Semantic colors: green for verified/online, amber for new match, red reserved for safety alerts only. Dark mode should maintain warmth — use warm dark gray, not cold black. Avoid: aggressive red that reads as danger instead of romance, cool-toned palettes that feel clinical, or backgrounds that clash with diverse skin tones in photos.
essential_ux: Safety and consent are foundational, not features — they must be woven into every interaction. Block and report must be accessible from any profile or conversation within one tap. Photo verification should be encouraged with clear trust badges. Unmatch must immediately end all contact with no message-after-unmatch loopholes. Location sharing should be opt-in with granular controls (neighborhood, not precise). Video chat should offer in-app options so users do not share personal phone numbers early. Profile prompts and icebreaker suggestions reduce blank-message syndrome and improve conversation quality. Avoid: dark patterns that manufacture urgency ("someone is looking at your profile right now"), paywalling basic safety features (blocking, reporting), notification spam designed to pull users back, or algorithmic deprioritization as punishment for inactivity.
ui_style_bias: Warm, vibrant UI; emphasizes photo-first profiles, smooth match interactions, and trust through verification

keywords: credentials, badges, certification, micro-credential, verification, digital badge, achievement, skills
visual_style: Clean, trustworthy, and achievement-oriented. Layouts must clearly communicate credential legitimacy and issuer authority. Typography should feel professional and institutional without being stuffy — clean sans-serifs with strong hierarchy. Badge and credential displays need consistent, recognizable visual patterns. Avoid playful or gamified aesthetics that undermine professional credibility.
landing_page: Landing page must immediately communicate credential value: what earners gain, how employers verify, and which issuers participate. Show recognizable issuer logos and sample credential displays. Below the fold: verification process explanation, integration partnerships (LinkedIn, HR systems), and earner testimonials with career outcomes. For issuers: ROI data, setup simplicity, and compliance with open badge standards. Single CTA to explore credentials or start issuing. Avoid: abstract achievement graphics, hidden verification processes, or marketing that conflates gamification badges with professional credentials.
dashboard_layout: Earner dashboard foregrounds: earned credentials with status (active, expiring, expired), skills map or pathway progress, and sharing/verification tools. Each credential card shows issuer, date, expiry, and a one-click verify/share action. Evidence portfolio links supporting materials to specific credentials. For issuer dashboards: template builder, batch issuance, analytics (issuance volume, verification rates, earner engagement), and compliance reporting. Pathway builder shows prerequisite chains visually. Avoid: flat lists without visual hierarchy, credential cards that lack issuer context, or pathways that hide completion requirements.
color_palette: Professional, trust-anchored palette — deep blues and neutral grays as base. Gold or amber (#FFD700 or warm gold) as achievement accent for earned credentials and completion states. White or very light gray backgrounds. Semantic colors: green for verified/active, amber for expiring soon, red for expired/revoked. Issuer branding should be accommodated within credential cards without overriding platform consistency. Avoid: playful or bright palettes that undermine credentialing authority, dark themes that make credentials harder to screenshot for sharing, or excessive issuer color customization that fragments the visual system.
essential_ux: Credential verification must be instant, public, and require zero authentication from the verifier — a shared link or QR code resolves to a verification page showing issuer, criteria, evidence, and status. Expiry management must proactively notify earners before credentials lapse with clear renewal paths. LinkedIn and HR system integration should be one-click from the credential card. Badge imagery must follow Open Badges or CLR standards for interoperability. Bulk issuance for organizations must include preview and error checking before committing. Credential revocation must be auditable and communicate clearly to the earner. Avoid: verification processes that require account creation, credentials that cannot be exported or shared outside the platform, pathways without clear completion criteria, or badge designs that look identical across different achievement levels.
ui_style_bias: Professional, achievement-oriented UI; emphasizes credential trust, verification clarity, and institutional authority

keywords: knowledge base, documentation, docs, wiki, help center, faq, guide, reference, manual
visual_style: Search-first, content-dense, and typographically rigorous. Every layout decision must serve scannability and findability. Use generous line-height, clear heading hierarchy (4 levels max), and consistent content width (65-80 characters per line for readability). Code blocks, tables, and callouts must be visually distinct from body text. Navigation must be persistent and scannable. Avoid decorative elements, marketing aesthetics, or layouts that prioritize brand over content consumption.
landing_page: Landing page is effectively a search box with curated entry points. Surface top categories, popular articles, and recently updated content. Search must be prominent and functional — not decorative. For product documentation: show version selector and quick-start guide prominently. For help centers: surface common issues and contact escalation path. Single CTA: search or browse. Avoid: marketing hero sections that push content below the fold, hidden search, or landing pages that resemble product pages rather than knowledge portals.
dashboard_layout: Left sidebar navigation with collapsible category tree — always visible, always showing current position. Main content area has a fixed max-width for reading comfort. Right sidebar (optional) shows on-page table of contents with scroll-spy highlighting. Breadcrumbs for every page. Previous/next navigation at page bottom for sequential reading. Code blocks support syntax highlighting and one-click copy. Version switcher persistent in header or sidebar. Search results show title, breadcrumb path, and highlighted matching text. Avoid: navigation that collapses on scroll, content wider than 80ch, code blocks without copy buttons, or pages without clear section anchors.
color_palette: Minimal, content-serving palette. White or very light warm gray background for reading comfort. Near-black text (#1a1a1a or similar) with strong contrast. Primary accent color used only for links, active navigation states, and interactive elements — never decorative. Code block backgrounds slightly darker (light gray) with monospace text. Callout blocks use pale tinted backgrounds (blue for info, amber for warning, red for danger, green for success/tip). Avoid: colored backgrounds that cause eye fatigue during extended reading, low-contrast syntax highlighting, or brand-heavy color usage that competes with content.
essential_ux: Search quality is the make-or-break UX factor. Search must handle typos, partial matches, synonyms, and return results ranked by relevance with context snippets. Implement search analytics to identify gaps (queries with zero results indicate missing content). Navigation must support both explorers (browsing via sidebar) and seekers (searching for specific answers). Feedback mechanisms ("Was this helpful?") should be lightweight (thumbs up/down) and immediately visible, not gated behind forms. Content freshness indicators (last updated date) build trust. Print/PDF export should preserve formatting. Anchor links for every heading enable deep linking into specific sections. Version switching must not lose the user's current page position. Avoid: search that only matches titles, navigation without current-page indicators, pages without last-updated dates, or feedback mechanisms that require authentication.
ui_style_bias: Minimal, search-first UI; emphasizes typographic clarity, persistent navigation, and content scannability

keywords: hyperlocal, local, nearby, neighborhood, service, booking, provider, on-demand, location
visual_style: Map-forward, trust-anchored, and action-oriented. Layouts must balance geographic discovery with service provider details. Typography should be clear and functional — optimized for quick scanning of names, ratings, prices, and availability. Use familiar map interaction patterns. Avoid overly stylized map aesthetics or complex filtering that slows down the path from search to booking.
landing_page: Landing page opens with location detection or search, immediately surfacing nearby service categories and top-rated providers. Below the fold: how it works (3 steps: search, book, done), trust signals (vetting process, insurance, guarantees), and provider testimonials. Category browsing should be visual (icons + labels) and limited to top 8-12 categories before requiring search. Single CTA to search or book. Avoid: generic hero images without location context, hidden service areas, or marketing content that delays the user from finding a local provider.
dashboard_layout: Split-view layout: map on one side, provider list on the other — with responsive collapse to list-first on mobile. Provider cards show photo, name, rating (numerical + count), price range, distance, and availability indicator. Map pins cluster at zoom-out and expand on zoom-in with summary tooltips. Filters: service type, price range, availability (today/this week), rating minimum, distance radius. Provider detail view shows reviews, portfolio/photos, credentials, availability calendar, and booking action. Avoid: map-only views that hide provider details, list-only views that lose geographic context, or filters that require scrolling to apply.
color_palette: Neutral, professional base with trust-oriented primary accent (blue or teal). Map uses standard cartographic conventions — avoid custom map themes that sacrifice readability. Provider cards on white or very light backgrounds for clarity. Semantic colors: green for available/verified, amber for limited availability, red for unavailable/flagged. Rating stars in gold or amber. Category icons should use the primary accent consistently. Avoid: bright or playful palettes that undermine service professionalism, map overlays that reduce pin visibility, or provider card backgrounds that compete with profile photos.
essential_ux: Location accuracy and booking confidence are the primary UX constraints. Location detection must request permission clearly and fall back to manual entry gracefully — never block the experience on location denial. Service area boundaries must be honest: show when a provider does not cover the user's area rather than presenting irrelevant results. Provider availability must be real-time or clearly timestamped. Booking confirmation must include provider details, service description, date/time, price, and cancellation policy — all on one screen. Reviews must be verified (tied to completed bookings) and sortable by recency and relevance. Provider response time expectations should be set clearly. Support in-app messaging between user and provider with booking context attached. Avoid: showing providers outside the service area, stale availability data, booking flows that hide cancellation terms, or review systems that cannot distinguish verified from unverified reviews.
ui_style_bias: Map-forward, trust-anchored UI; emphasizes proximity discovery, provider credibility, and fast booking

keywords: beauty, spa, wellness, salon, massage, skincare, facial, nail, waxing, aesthetic, self-care, treatment
visual_style: Serene, sensory, and aspirational. Layouts should evoke calm and indulgence through generous whitespace, soft shapes, and high-quality imagery. Typography should feel elegant but readable — light-weight serifs or refined sans-serifs for headings, clean sans-serifs for body. Use imagery as a primary design element (treatments, environments, textures). Motion should be smooth and unhurried. Avoid clinical aesthetics, dense layouts, or aggressive sales-oriented patterns that break the relaxation promise.
landing_page: Landing page must evoke the in-person experience visually — lead with atmospheric photography of the space and treatments, not stock models. Communicate core services, location, and booking availability above the fold. Below the fold: service menu with pricing (never hide prices), before/after gallery (with client consent), practitioner credentials, and client testimonials. Single CTA for booking — always visible, never competing with secondary actions. Gift card and package options should be discoverable but not dominating. Avoid: auto-playing background music, hero carousels that delay booking access, or landing pages that feel like product catalogs rather than invitations.
dashboard_layout: Service menu is the primary navigation hub — organized by category (face, body, nails, packages) with clear pricing, duration, and brief descriptions. Booking flow must show real-time practitioner availability with calendar view, allow service add-ons during booking (not after), and confirm total price before submission. Client profile stores preferences, allergies, treatment history, and rebooking shortcuts. Loyalty/membership status visible on dashboard with clear benefit tracking. Gallery section should be filterable by service type. Avoid: booking flows longer than 3 steps, service menus without pricing, practitioner selection without photos/bios, or membership terms hidden in fine print.
color_palette: Soft, luxurious palette — muted blush, sage, cream, warm taupe, or soft lavender as primary tones depending on brand positioning. Background warm off-white or cream, never stark white. Accent color used sparingly for CTAs and active states — rose gold, soft gold, or deep botanical green work well. Imagery should drive the color story. Semantic colors softened: muted green for confirmed, warm amber for pending, soft rose for cancellation. Dark mode is generally unnecessary for this category — the warm, light aesthetic is the brand. Avoid: high-saturation colors that feel clinical or energetic, dark backgrounds that undermine the calming atmosphere, or palettes that clash with treatment photography.
essential_ux: Booking convenience is the primary UX driver — users should go from landing to confirmed appointment in under 60 seconds for returning clients. Rebooking recent services must be one-tap. Cancellation and rescheduling policies must be stated clearly during booking, not buried in terms. Intake forms for new clients (allergies, skin conditions, preferences) should be completable on mobile before arrival. Appointment reminders should include preparation instructions (arrive early, avoid certain products). Before/after galleries must obtain and display consent clearly. Reviews should be tied to verified visits. Gift card purchase and redemption must be frictionless — no codes to manually enter if digital. Avoid: booking systems that require calling for availability, intake forms that repeat questions for returning clients, hidden cancellation fees, or photo galleries that use client images without visible consent.
ui_style_bias: Serene, sensory UI; emphasizes atmospheric imagery, effortless booking, and soft luxurious tones

keywords: luxury, premium, brand, exclusive, high-end, designer, couture, bespoke, prestige
visual_style: Cinematic, editorial, and restrained. Every design choice must reinforce exclusivity and craftsmanship. Use dramatic whitespace, oversized typography for statements, and controlled asymmetry. Imagery must be art-directed — never stock. Motion should be smooth, deliberate, and purposeful, enhancing the sense of precision. Layouts should feel curated and intentional, never busy. Avoid trends that date quickly, generic UI patterns, or any element that dilutes the perception of scarcity and quality.
landing_page: Landing page is an editorial experience — lead with a full-bleed hero featuring a single product or campaign image with minimal text overlay. The brand story unfolds through scrolling, not through feature lists. Below the fold: curated collections (3-5 max), craftsmanship narrative with close-up product details, and heritage/provenance section. CTA is understated but clear — "Explore the Collection" or "Request an Appointment" rather than aggressive "Buy Now". For brands with physical locations: boutique finder prominently placed. Social proof is implicit through brand heritage, press features, and celebrity association — never user-generated star ratings. Avoid: discount banners, pop-up modals, chatbot widgets, urgency timers, or any element that cheapens the perception.
dashboard_layout: Navigation should be minimal (4-6 items max) with clean typography — mega-menus only if the catalog demands it, and even then, restrained and image-rich. Product pages are editorial spreads: multiple high-resolution images with zoom capability, detailed material/craftsmanship descriptions, and sizing/care information. Product grids use generous spacing with 2-3 columns maximum. Shopping bag replaces "cart" in language. Wishlist and save functionality available without creating an account. For appointment-based brands: scheduling interface should feel personal and concierge-like, not transactional. Avoid: dense product grids, aggressive cross-sell modules, cluttered filters, or UX patterns borrowed from mass-market e-commerce.
color_palette: Black, white, and one signature brand accent define the palette. Background is either pure white with dramatic dark type, or rich dark (near-black, deep navy) with light type — never gray or mid-tone backgrounds that feel indecisive. Gold, champagne, or deep burgundy as accent for interactive elements and highlights. Product photography backgrounds must be consistent and complementary. Typography color maintains maximum contrast. Semantic colors are minimal and muted — confirmations in subtle green, errors in soft red, never alarming. Dark mode is the natural state for many luxury brands; light mode should feel equally intentional. Avoid: gradients, bright accent colors, colored backgrounds that compete with products, or palette choices that signal mass-market positioning.
essential_ux: The luxury UX paradox: the experience must feel effortless while maintaining an aura of exclusivity. Page load performance is critical — slow loading destroys the illusion of quality (perceived performance directly maps to perceived brand quality). Images must be high-resolution but optimized; use progressive loading that reveals beauty, not placeholder boxes. Product discovery should feel curated, not algorithmic — editorial recommendations over "customers also bought." Checkout must be seamless with minimal form fields, address auto-complete, and premium payment options (Apple Pay, concierge ordering). Packaging and delivery expectations should be set clearly — luxury customers expect premium unboxing. Returns must be handled gracefully with prepaid labels and no-questions policies communicated upfront. Personalization should feel like a concierge relationship, not surveillance — "Your stylist recommends" over "Based on your browsing history." Avoid: generic recommendation engines, pop-up discount offers, CAPTCHA on checkout, aggressive email capture modals, or any friction that contradicts the promise of premium service.
ui_style_bias: Cinematic, editorial UI; emphasizes craftsmanship, dramatic whitespace, and restrained exclusivity

keywords: restaurant, food, dining, menu, order, delivery, reservation, takeout, cuisine, catering
visual_style: Warm, appetizing, and action-oriented. Food photography must drive the visual experience — layouts should frame images generously with warm lighting tones. Typography should feel inviting and readable at menu-scanning speed — avoid decorative scripts that sacrifice legibility. Use modular blocks for menu categories. Motion should be subtle and purposeful (cart updates, order confirmations). Avoid cold, corporate aesthetics or overly minimal designs that strip the sensory appeal from food.
landing_page: Landing page must answer three questions instantly: what cuisine, how to order, and where/when. Hero features high-quality food photography — not the restaurant exterior. Menu or top dishes visible without scrolling. Location, hours, and ordering options (dine-in, takeout, delivery) prominent above the fold. Below the fold: full menu preview, reservation widget, and delivery radius or third-party app links. Single primary CTA — "Order Now" or "Reserve a Table" depending on business model. Avoid: hero carousels of generic food stock photos, menus available only as PDF downloads, or hidden hours and location.
dashboard_layout: Menu is the primary interface — organized by category (appetizers, mains, desserts) with item photos, descriptions, dietary tags (vegetarian, gluten-free, spicy level), and prices always visible. For ordering: cart persists across navigation, item customization (toppings, sides, special instructions) is inline not modal, and order total updates in real-time. For reservations: date/time/party-size selector with instant availability confirmation. Order tracking shows clear status progression (confirmed, preparing, ready/en-route). Avoid: menus without prices, item customization flows longer than 2 steps, order tracking that requires page refresh, or PDF-only menus that break mobile usability.
color_palette: Warm, appetite-stimulating palette — deep oranges, warm reds, rich browns, and cream as the base spectrum. Background warm white or light cream to let food photography pop. Accent color for CTAs and cart indicators. Dietary and allergen tags use consistent, subdued color coding (green for vegetarian, amber for contains allergens). Avoid: cool blues or clinical whites that suppress appetite (color psychology research consistently links warm tones to food appeal), dark themes that diminish food photography quality, or neon accents that feel fast-food generic.
essential_ux: Speed and clarity drive conversion — users decide and order quickly or abandon. Menu load time is critical; lazy-load images but never show empty placeholder grids. Dietary and allergen information must be filterable, not just labeled — users with restrictions need to narrow the menu, not scan every item. Special instructions field must be prominent and generous (not a tiny text input). Delivery estimates must be honest and updated in real-time — overpromising and underdelivering destroys trust faster than a longer honest estimate. Tipping interface should present fair defaults without dark patterns (pre-selected high percentages, guilt-inducing copy). Reservation confirmations must include cancellation policy and modification options. For multi-location brands: location selector must auto-detect or prompt clearly, never serve a menu for the wrong location. Avoid: menus that require zooming on mobile, checkout flows that add fees at the last step, order minimums hidden until cart review, or reservation systems that do not send confirmation emails/texts.
ui_style_bias: Warm, appetizing UI; emphasizes food photography, fast ordering, and clear menu hierarchy

keywords: fitness, gym, workout, exercise, training, health, strength, cardio, yoga, CrossFit
visual_style: Energetic, motivational, and performance-driven. Dark mode default suits focused workout sessions and reduces glare in gym environments. Layouts must surface active workout state prominently with large, glanceable typography for reps, sets, and timers. Use bold contrast and dynamic elements that reinforce energy without distracting during exercise. Avoid overly decorative or playful aesthetics that undermine the serious training mindset — the UI is a tool, not entertainment.
landing_page: Landing page must communicate the training philosophy and target audience immediately — generic "get fit" messaging fails to differentiate. Show the core workout experience (app screenshots during a session, not just marketing renders). Below the fold: sample workout plans, progress examples with real metrics, and trainer/methodology credentials. For gym apps: class schedule, facility info, and membership pricing visible without scrolling. Single CTA to start a free workout or trial. Avoid: before/after body transformation photos as primary marketing (body-shaming concerns), hidden pricing, or landing pages that look identical to every other fitness app.
dashboard_layout: Active workout screen is the hero — timer, current exercise with form guidance (video or illustration), rep/set counter, and rest period timer must be visible simultaneously without scrolling. Navigation during workout must be minimal (pause, skip, end). Workout library organized by type (strength, cardio, flexibility, HIIT), muscle group, duration, and difficulty. Progress dashboard shows key metrics: workout frequency, volume trends, personal records, and streak (with forgiving streak logic — missed days should not reset months of progress). Calendar view for workout history and scheduling. For gym/class apps: schedule with real-time availability, waitlist, and check-in. Avoid: cluttered workout screens that require scrolling mid-exercise, progress dashboards that only show weight/body metrics (train metrics over body metrics), or workout libraries without clear difficulty indicators.
color_palette: Dark background default (near-black or very dark charcoal) with high-energy accent — electric blue, vibrant orange, or neon green depending on brand energy. White or light gray text with strong contrast for readability in varied lighting (bright gym, outdoor, dark bedroom). Timer and active exercise elements use the accent color for emphasis. Progress charts use the accent spectrum. Rest period screens can dim slightly to signal pause. Semantic colors: green for completed/PR, amber for in-progress, red for skipped or missed. Light mode alternative for users who prefer it, maintaining the same energy. Avoid: low-contrast text that is unreadable in bright gym lighting, pure black backgrounds that feel lifeless, or pastel palettes that undermine workout intensity.
essential_ux: Mid-workout usability is the critical constraint — users interact with sweaty hands, limited attention, and time pressure. Touch targets must be oversized (minimum 48px, ideally larger). Workout controls (pause, skip, complete set) must be accessible with one hand. Auto-lock prevention during active workouts is essential. Timer audio cues supplement visual indicators for users who cannot watch the screen. Rest period timers should auto-start and provide haptic/audio alerts. Exercise form guidance (video, animation, or cues) prevents injury and builds confidence — this is a safety feature, not a nice-to-have. Progress tracking should celebrate consistency over intensity — streaks that forgive occasional misses, personal records highlighted automatically, and gentle re-engagement after breaks (not guilt). Offline support for workout execution is mandatory — gym connectivity is unreliable. Sync when back online seamlessly. Avoid: tiny buttons during active workouts, mandatory internet for workout playback, guilt-based re-engagement notifications ("You've been inactive for 5 days!"), or progress metrics that only track body weight.
ui_style_bias: Dark, energetic UI; emphasizes glanceable workout data, bold contrast, and motivational progress cues

keywords: real estate, property, housing, rent, buy, sell, listing, apartment, mortgage, agent, broker, home
visual_style: Trust-forward, image-rich, and search-driven. Layouts must balance large property photography with structured listing data (price, beds, baths, sqft, location). Typography should be clean and confident — optimized for scanning numerical data and addresses. Map integration is core, not supplementary. Avoid flashy or trendy aesthetics that distract from the largest financial decision most users will make.
landing_page: Landing page opens with a prominent search bar (location, buy/rent toggle, price range) — this is the primary action, not a hero image. Below the search: featured listings with high-quality photos, neighborhood spotlights, and market insights (median prices, trends). For agent sites: credentials, sold history, and client testimonials. Single CTA to search or contact an agent. Mortgage calculator or affordability tool should be discoverable but secondary. Avoid: auto-playing video tours on landing, hero images without search functionality, or hiding the buy/rent distinction behind navigation.
dashboard_layout: Search results in split-view: map with listing pins on one side, scrollable listing cards on the other. Listing cards show lead photo, price, key specs (bed/bath/sqft), address, and days-on-market. Map pins display price on hover. Saved searches and favorites must persist across sessions without requiring sign-up for basic use. Property detail pages: photo gallery with intuitive swipe/grid toggle, virtual tour embed, property details in scannable sections (not paragraphs), neighborhood data (schools, transit, walkability scores), price history, and clear contact/schedule-tour CTA. For agent dashboards: pipeline view of leads, showing activity, and listing performance metrics. Avoid: listing cards without photos, property pages that bury square footage or lot size, map views without price indicators, or search results that cannot be sorted by multiple criteria.
color_palette: Professional, trust-anchored palette — deep blue or navy as primary, warm gold or amber as accent for CTAs and featured badges. Background white or very light gray to let property photography dominate. Map uses standard cartographic styling for readability. Price and status indicators: green for new/reduced, amber for pending, red for sold/off-market. Agent branding accommodated subtly within listing cards. Dark mode optional but property photos must render accurately in both modes. Avoid: colored backgrounds that cast tints on property photos, playful or casual palettes that undermine the gravity of the transaction, or status colors that are ambiguous (e.g., using blue for both links and pending status).
essential_ux: Property search is the primary UX — search must support natural-language-like inputs ("3 bed under 500k near downtown"), saved searches with notifications for new matches, and map-draw custom boundaries. Photo quality makes or breaks listings; support high-resolution galleries with fast loading (progressive JPEG, lazy load). Virtual tours must load quickly and work on mobile without app installation. Contact forms must clearly set response-time expectations. Mortgage/affordability calculators should use current rates and update dynamically. Listing freshness is critical — clearly display days-on-market and last-updated timestamps; stale listings erode platform trust. Comparison tools (side-by-side properties) reduce decision fatigue. For renters: application status tracking, document upload, and lease review tools. Avoid: requiring account creation before viewing listings, contact forms that hide which agent responds, photo galleries without clear unit counts, or school/transit data that cannot be verified against authoritative sources.
ui_style_bias: Trust-forward, image-rich UI; emphasizes property search, map integration, and transparent listing data

keywords: travel, tourism, vacation, flight, hotel, booking, destination, trip, itinerary, resort, tour
visual_style: Aspirational, immersive, and discovery-oriented. Layouts must balance inspirational destination imagery with practical booking mechanics. Typography should feel modern and confident — readable across dense itinerary data and evocative in editorial contexts. Use full-bleed photography and smooth transitions to evoke wanderlust, but ensure booking flows are efficient and distraction-free. Avoid generic stock imagery or cluttered interfaces that reduce travel to a transaction.
landing_page: Landing page must inspire and enable simultaneously — hero with stunning destination imagery and an integrated search bar (destination, dates, travelers). Below the fold: curated destination collections, seasonal deals with transparent pricing (total price, not per-night buried fees), and editorial content (travel guides, itineraries). Social proof via traveler reviews with photos, not just star ratings. For tour operators: highlight unique experiences, group sizes, and guide expertise. Single CTA to search or explore deals. Avoid: pop-up deal alerts, hidden resort fees revealed at checkout, or hero sections that prioritize airline/hotel branding over destinations.
dashboard_layout: Search results must show total price including all fees and taxes — never a base rate that inflates at checkout. Listing cards: lead photo, destination, dates, total price, and key differentiators (free cancellation, breakfast included, rating). Filters for price range, star rating, amenities, cancellation policy, and distance to landmarks. Comparison view for shortlisted options. Itinerary builder organizes bookings chronologically with map visualization of the route. Booking detail pages: room/flight specifics, cancellation terms, included amenities, and traveler reviews inline. For multi-segment trips: clear per-segment pricing and cross-sell (car rental, activities) that is helpful, not aggressive. Avoid: search results sorted by commission rather than relevance, price displays that exclude mandatory fees, or itinerary views that cannot be shared or exported.
color_palette: Destination-adaptive palette strategy — the platform chrome stays neutral (clean whites, warm grays, confident navy or dark charcoal for headers) while destination photography drives the emotional color story. Primary accent for CTAs and interactive elements — warm coral, ocean blue, or sunset amber depending on brand positioning. Price and deal tags use a consistent highlight color (warm gold or bright accent). Semantic colors: green for available/free cancellation, amber for limited availability, red for sold out or non-refundable. Map styling clean and readable. Avoid: busy patterns or gradients that compete with destination photography, cool corporate palettes that drain the aspirational warmth, or inconsistent accent colors across different booking stages.
essential_ux: Price transparency is the single biggest trust factor — display total costs including taxes, fees, and mandatory charges from the first search result. Drip pricing (revealing fees progressively through checkout) is the most-cited reason travelers abandon bookings and distrust platforms. Cancellation policies must be stated in plain language with specific dates ("Free cancellation until March 15") not vague terms ("flexible"). Date picker must support flexible-date search (cheapest in month, weekend trips) and clearly show price variation by date. Multi-currency and timezone handling must be automatic with clear labeling. Booking confirmation must include all essential details on one screen and via email: confirmation number, dates, address, cancellation terms, and emergency contact. Travel document requirements (visa, passport validity, vaccination) should surface proactively for international destinations. Saved trips and wishlists must sync across devices. Avoid: drip pricing, checkout flows that add fees in final steps, date pickers that do not show price variation, or booking confirmations that lack cancellation instructions.
ui_style_bias: Aspirational, immersive UI; emphasizes destination photography, transparent pricing, and seamless booking flow

keywords: hotel, hospitality, resort, lodge, inn, boutique hotel, guest, accommodation, booking, stay
visual_style: Warm, polished, and confidence-building. Layouts must showcase rooms and amenities through high-quality photography while keeping booking mechanics fast and predictable. Typography should feel refined and hospitable — warm sans-serifs or elegant serifs for headings, clean sans-serifs for rates and details. Every screen should reinforce the feeling of being welcomed, not sold to. Avoid cold transactional aesthetics or over-designed interfaces that slow the path from browsing to booking.
landing_page: Landing page leads with the property's signature visual — hero image of the defining space (lobby, pool, view, signature room) with integrated date/guest search. Below the fold: room categories with lead photos and starting rates, amenities grid with icons, location context (map, nearby attractions, transit), and guest reviews. For chains: property selector with location search. Seasonal or promotional rates should be visible but not dominating. Single CTA to check availability. Avoid: auto-rotating hero carousels that delay search, hidden total pricing, room descriptions without photos, or burying the location and contact information.
dashboard_layout: Room selection presents categories with photo galleries, rate comparison (flexible vs. non-refundable), amenity lists, and occupancy limits. Calendar-based availability must show rate variation by date and highlight minimum-stay requirements upfront. Booking summary persists during the flow showing room, dates, rate, taxes, and total — updated in real-time as add-ons are selected. Upsell opportunities (room upgrades, breakfast, spa packages, late checkout) presented as helpful suggestions at appropriate moments, not aggressive interstitials. Guest portal post-booking: reservation details, check-in/out times, pre-arrival requests (pillow preference, early check-in), and digital key where supported. For property dashboards: occupancy calendar, revenue per available room, guest communication log, and housekeeping status. Avoid: booking flows longer than 3 steps, rate calendars that hide fees until checkout, upsell modals that block the booking path, or post-booking portals that require a separate account from the booking.
color_palette: Warm, welcoming palette — cream, warm taupe, and soft gold as the foundation. Primary accent in deep warm tones (burgundy, forest green, or navy) depending on property positioning. Gold or champagne for premium indicators and CTAs. Background warm off-white, never stark or clinical. Photography backgrounds should feel consistent and true to the property's actual lighting. Rate displays use clear, high-contrast typography. Semantic colors: green for available, amber for limited rooms, red for sold out. Seasonal or promotional rates highlighted with a warm accent tag, not aggressive red sale badges. Avoid: cool corporate blues that feel like an OTA rather than a property, dark themes that diminish room photography, or inconsistent color temperature between marketing imagery and actual property photos.
essential_ux: Rate transparency builds booking confidence — display total cost including taxes, resort fees, and mandatory charges from the availability view, not at checkout. This is the single highest-impact trust factor; hidden fees are the top reason guests book through OTAs instead of direct. Cancellation policy must be stated in plain language with specific deadline dates on the booking summary. Date flexibility tools (cheapest night indicator, flexible date search) reduce abandonment. Room photography must be accurate and current — misrepresentation causes negative reviews disproportionate to the actual shortcoming. Check-in/out process should be streamable digitally with clear timing expectations. Guest communication (pre-arrival, during stay, post-checkout) should be proactive but not intrusive — one confirmation email, one pre-arrival details email, one post-stay feedback request. Accessibility information (ADA rooms, elevator access, service animal policy) must be findable without contacting the property. Loyalty program status and benefits should be visible throughout the booking flow for members. Avoid: resort fee disclosure only at checkout, room photos that misrepresent size or view, mandatory phone calls for modifications, or feedback requests before the guest has checked out.
ui_style_bias: Warm, polished UI; emphasizes property photography, transparent rates, and hospitable booking confidence

keywords: wedding, event planning, bridal, ceremony, celebration, party, planner, reception, nuptial, event coordinator
visual_style: Elegant and warm with a soft, romantic sensibility. Typography should lean editorial — use serif or semi-serif headings paired with clean body text. Layouts should feel curated, not cluttered. Generous whitespace and soft color transitions create a premium, aspirational feel. Photography should be large and emotive. Avoid: corporate stiffness, overly playful elements, and anything that feels mass-market. The tone should feel personal and bespoke.
landing_page: Hero should feature aspirational event photography — a real moment, not staged perfection. Lead with emotional messaging that speaks to the experience, not a feature list. Below the fold: portfolio gallery organized by event type or style, a concise services overview, and a testimonials section with couple names and photos. Pricing should be presented as starting-from tiers or a consultation CTA — avoid rigid pricing grids. A planning timeline or process overview builds confidence. Vendor partnerships can be shown subtly. CTA should invite consultation, not hard-sell.
dashboard_layout: If a client portal exists, organize around the event timeline — a visual timeline of milestones (venue, catering, florals, etc.) with completion status. Checklist functionality with due dates and assignment. Budget tracker with category breakdown and remaining balance. Vendor contact directory. Shared inspiration board or mood board area. Document storage for contracts and proposals. Avoid: complex dashboards with charts — wedding planning is task-driven, not analytics-driven.
color_palette: Soft, warm palette with romantic undertones. Use muted pinks, sage greens, warm creams, and gold accents — avoid saturated or neon tones. The palette should feel timeless rather than trendy. Reserve gold or rose gold for premium accents and CTAs. Backgrounds should be warm white or soft cream, never stark white. Ensure the palette works with diverse photography — it should complement, not compete with, client imagery.
essential_ux: Trust and emotional connection drive conversions. Social proof through real event galleries is more persuasive than testimonials alone. The booking/inquiry flow should be warm and low-friction — avoid long forms; a name, date, and message are sufficient for first contact. Image-heavy pages must load fast on mobile — most couples browse on phones during commutes and downtime. Gallery filtering by event type, style, or venue helps visitors self-qualify. Accessibility matters: ensure all images have meaningful alt text and navigation is keyboard-accessible.
ui_style_bias: Soft, editorial elegance; warm tones, serif headings, romantic imagery, gold accents, and curated whitespace

keywords: legal, law, attorney, lawyer, law firm, litigation, legal services, compliance, counsel, solicitor
visual_style: Authoritative and restrained. Typography should convey gravitas — use a strong serif for headings and a highly readable sans-serif for body. Color usage should be conservative and deliberate. Layouts should be structured and predictable; avoid anything that feels experimental or casual. Whitespace and alignment communicate discipline. Photography should show real people in professional settings, not generic handshake stock photos. The overall tone should say competent and trustworthy, not innovative and disruptive.
landing_page: Lead with the firm's core differentiator in one clear sentence — what type of law and why this firm. Practice areas should be prominently displayed as clickable categories with brief descriptions. Attorney profiles with credentials, headshots, and areas of expertise build trust. Include a results or case outcomes section with quantified impact where possible. Trust signals: bar associations, awards, years of practice. CTA should be Schedule a Consultation — never Get Started or Sign Up. Contact information must be visible on every page. Avoid: animated heroes, informal tone, and pricing information since legal pricing is case-specific.
dashboard_layout: Client portals should organize around the active case. Display case status with clear stage indicators (intake, discovery, negotiation, resolution). Document management with version control and secure sharing. Communication log showing all correspondence. Billing section with detailed time entries, invoices, and payment status. Calendar integration for court dates, deadlines, and meetings. Secure messaging between client and attorney. Avoid: complex dashboards with analytics — clients want case progress, not metrics.
color_palette: Navy blue as primary conveys authority and trust. Gold or warm brass accents add prestige without ostentation. Background should be clean white or light warm grey. Text colors should maximize readability — near-black body text, never medium grey. Limit the palette to 3-4 colors maximum. Avoid: bright blues that feel tech-startup, greens that imply finance, and any color that reduces perceived seriousness. Semantic colors for alerts should be used sparingly.
essential_ux: Trust and credibility are the only things that matter. Every design choice should reduce anxiety and communicate competence. Navigation must be predictable and shallow — practice areas, attorneys, about, contact. Page load speed matters for SEO and first impressions. Attorney profiles are the highest-traffic pages after the homepage; invest in their quality. Forms should be short and clearly indicate confidentiality. Mobile optimization is critical — potential clients often search for legal help on personal devices. Accessibility compliance (WCAG AA) is both ethical and legally prudent for a law firm.
ui_style_bias: Authoritative, restrained design; serif headings, navy palette, structured layouts, conservative typography, and trust-first hierarchy

keywords: insurance, policy, coverage, claims, underwriting, premium, insurance platform, insure, risk, actuary
visual_style: Clean, professional, and reassuring. The visual language should communicate stability and reliability without feeling old-fashioned.
