Typography should be highly readable and accessible — avoid thin weights and small sizes. Use structured layouts with clear sections and generous padding. Illustration style (if used) should be clean and informative, not whimsical. The interface should feel approachable but not casual — insurance is serious business, and the design should respect that while reducing intimidation.
landing_page: Hero should present a clear value proposition: what kind of insurance and the primary benefit (savings, coverage breadth, speed of claims). Below the fold: product comparison showing plans side-by-side with honest feature matrices. A quote calculator or zip-code-based CTA drives conversion. Trust signals are essential: financial ratings, regulatory compliance, number of customers served, years in business. FAQ section addressing common objections (cost, coverage gaps, claims process). Testimonials should focus on claims experiences, not just price. Avoid: fear-based messaging, fine-print disclaimers in hero sections, and complex jargon.
dashboard_layout: Policy overview as the primary view: active policies, coverage amounts, renewal dates, and payment status at a glance. Claims section with clear status tracking (submitted, under review, approved, paid) and expected timelines. Document center for policy documents, ID cards, and correspondence. Quick-action buttons for filing a claim, making a payment, and contacting support. Billing history with downloadable statements. Avoid: information overload — surface critical details and let users drill down. Progressive disclosure for policy details.
color_palette: Trust blue as primary — it communicates reliability and calm. Green as secondary for positive states (active, approved, covered). Use amber sparingly for warnings (renewal approaching, coverage gap). Backgrounds should be clean and light. Avoid: red as a dominant color (triggers anxiety in insurance context), dark themes (reduce transparency perception), and overly vibrant accents. Ensure high contrast for all text, especially for older users who index higher in insurance markets.
essential_ux: Clarity and anxiety reduction drive every UX decision. Insurance jargon must be translated to plain language — use tooltips or inline definitions for technical terms. The quote-to-purchase flow should be completable in under 5 minutes. Progress indicators for multi-step processes are mandatory. Claims filing must be frictionless: pre-fill known information, support photo uploads for documentation, and confirm receipt immediately. Comparison tools should be honest and clear — never hide exclusions. Accessibility is critical given the broad age range of insurance customers. Performance must be fast, especially for quote calculators.
ui_style_bias: Clean, stable interface; trust-building blue palette, clear comparison layouts, reassuring feedback states, and accessible type scale

keywords: banking, bank, finance, traditional finance, checking, savings, mortgage, loan, credit, financial services
visual_style: Institutional-grade with modern clarity. The design must convey security, stability, and competence above all else. Typography should be precise and legible — use a professional sans-serif with strong weight hierarchy. Layouts should be grid-aligned and predictable. Every pixel should feel intentional. Avoid: trendy design patterns, playful elements, and anything that suggests impermanence. The interface should feel secure, organized, and trustworthy. Density should be medium-high for account views.
landing_page: Lead with the primary product (checking, savings, or lending) and its key differentiator (rates, fees, accessibility). Product cards should show concrete numbers — APY, fees, minimums — not vague promises. Comparison table for account tiers. Security section is non-negotiable: FDIC insurance, encryption badges, regulatory affiliations. Mobile app showcase with real screenshots. Branch/ATM locator for institutions with physical presence. CTA is Open an Account with estimated time to complete. Avoid: lifestyle imagery that says nothing about the product, hidden fees, and jargon-heavy descriptions.
dashboard_layout: Account summary as the default view: all accounts with current balances, recent transactions, and available funds. Transaction list should support search, filtering by date/amount/category, and export. Transfer functionality must be prominent and predictable — clearly show source, destination, amount, and timing. Bill pay and scheduled transactions in a dedicated section. Alerts and notifications for low balance, large transactions, and security events. Spending insights with category breakdowns can be valuable but should be secondary to account management. Avoid: cramming all features into the sidebar — use progressive disclosure.
color_palette: Navy or dark blue as primary communicates institutional trust. White and light grey backgrounds ensure readability for dense financial data. Green for positive balances and deposits, red for withdrawals and overdrafts — these conventions are deeply learned and should not be subverted. Gold accents for premium tiers. Avoid: bright colors that feel frivolous, dark mode as default (transparency concerns), and gradients or decorative color usage. All color coding must be paired with non-color indicators for accessibility.
essential_ux: Security perception and data accuracy are paramount. Every transaction should confirm before executing and provide clear receipts. Session timeouts must be handled gracefully with save-state on sensitive forms. Authentication should support biometrics and MFA without adding excessive friction. Error messages must be specific and actionable — never show vague failure states. Performance is critical for account data — stale balance displays erode trust. Accessibility (WCAG AA minimum) is both a legal requirement and a user necessity given broad demographics. Print-friendly views for statements and tax documents. Zero tolerance for layout shifts — financial data must never jump on screen.
ui_style_bias: Institutional precision; navy palette, grid-locked layouts, security-forward chrome, high-contrast financial data, and zero decorative friction

keywords: online course, e-learning, mooc, course platform, certification, curriculum, instructor, lms, training, upskilling
visual_style: Content-focused and motivational without being distracting. Typography should prioritize readability for long-form content — generous line height, moderate line length (60-80 characters), and clear heading hierarchy. Use consistent, repeated layout patterns for lessons so learners build spatial memory. Visual design should recede behind content: clean backgrounds, subtle borders, and restrained color. Video player and reading areas need maximum breathing room. Avoid: heavy branding that competes with course content, and decorative elements that add no informational value.
landing_page: Hero should present the course outcome, not the platform features — lead with what learners will become or achieve, with a specific timeframe if applicable. Course catalog below the fold with filtering by topic, level, and format. Each course card shows: title, instructor, duration, rating, and enrollment count. Social proof via completion rates and career outcomes outweighs testimonials. Pricing should be transparent — show per-course and subscription options clearly. A free preview or sample lesson is the highest-converting CTA. Instructor credentials visible on landing pages. Avoid: vague promises, stock photos of people at laptops, and hiding the price.
dashboard_layout: Learner dashboard should foreground the current course with clear progress and a Continue Learning action as the dominant element. Course library as secondary navigation. Progress tracking should show both completion percentage and estimated time remaining. Certificate/achievement section for completed courses. Calendar or schedule view for live sessions and deadlines. Notes and bookmarks accessible from the dashboard. Recommendation section based on completed courses. Avoid: social features dominating the learning interface, and metrics that shame slow learners.
color_palette: Use a calming, focused palette — medium blue or teal as primary conveys learning and trust. Progress indicators should use a consistent warm color (amber or green) that feels rewarding. Category colors can differentiate course topics but should be muted to avoid visual chaos. Video player surroundings should be dark or neutral to reduce glare. Background should be warm white for reading comfort. Avoid: high-saturation palettes that cause eye fatigue during long study sessions, and dark themes as default for text-heavy content.
essential_ux: Completion rate is the north-star metric — every UX decision should reduce dropout. Video player must be robust: adjustable speed, captions, bookmarking, and resume-from-last-position. Mobile learning is critical — ensure video and text content adapt seamlessly. Offline access for downloaded lessons. Progress should auto-save aggressively — losing position is the fastest way to lose a learner. Search should span all course content, not just titles. Certificate generation should be instant upon completion. Accessibility: captions for all video, screen reader support for quizzes, and keyboard navigation throughout. Page performance matters for global audiences on slow connections.
ui_style_bias: Content-first learning layout; calm palette, readable typography, prominent progress tracking, distraction-free video, and motivational feedback cues

keywords: nonprofit, non-profit, charity, ngo, foundation, cause, donation, philanthropy, volunteer, social impact
visual_style: Warm, authentic, and mission-driven. The visual language should evoke empathy and trust without manipulation. Photography should be real and respectful — show the people and communities served with dignity, never as objects of pity. Typography should be clean and accessible with clear hierarchy. Layouts should be open and inviting, with generous whitespace. Color usage should be warm and grounded. Avoid: corporate polish that feels disconnected from the mission, stock photography, and design patterns borrowed from e-commerce that treat donors as customers.
landing_page: Open with the mission in one powerful sentence, paired with authentic photography or a short video. Impact metrics below the fold — concrete numbers (meals served, homes built, students supported) are more compelling than narrative alone. A clearly visible donation CTA that stays accessible throughout the page but does not feel aggressive. Transparency section showing how funds are allocated with a simple breakdown. Volunteer opportunities and ways to get involved beyond donating. Upcoming events or campaigns. Trust signals: charity ratings, annual report links, board of directors. Avoid: guilt-driven messaging, autoplay videos, and donation CTAs that feel like pop-up ads.
dashboard_layout: If a donor portal exists, show impact over time: total contributions, projects supported, and tangible outcomes from their giving. Recurring donation management with easy modification. Tax receipt history and downloadable statements. Event calendar for volunteer opportunities. Newsletter archive or impact updates. Keep it simple — most nonprofit supporters do not need a complex dashboard. The focus should be on connection to impact, not data management.
color_palette: Warm, earthy tones as primary — deep greens, warm oranges, or cause-specific colors that connect to the mission. Avoid cold, corporate blues unless the nonprofit is in healthcare or education. Gold or amber accents for CTAs and donation buttons convey generosity. Background should be warm white or soft cream. Ensure high contrast for accessibility — nonprofit audiences span all demographics and ability levels. Use color sparingly and meaningfully; the photography and content should carry emotional weight, not the palette.
essential_ux: The donation flow is the critical path — it must be completable in under 60 seconds. Support multiple amounts (preset and custom), recurring options, and at least 3 payment methods. Show impact equivalency to make giving tangible (e.g. a specific dollar amount funds a specific outcome). Tax receipt should be generated instantly. Page load speed matters for global audiences on mobile. Transparency builds trust: make financial reports, program details, and leadership information easy to find. Accessibility (WCAG AA) is a moral imperative for mission-driven organizations. Email capture for non-donors should be gentle and offer genuine value through impact updates.
ui_style_bias: Warm, mission-driven design; authentic photography, earthy tones, transparent impact metrics, dignified imagery, and gentle conversion paths

keywords: music, streaming, audio, playlist, songs, albums, artists, podcast, radio, listening
visual_style: Immersive and content-forward with dark-mode-first design. The UI should recede behind album art and artist imagery — chrome should be minimal and semi-transparent where possible. Typography should be clean and legible against dark backgrounds with sufficient weight contrast. Layout density should be high to support browsing large libraries without excessive scrolling. Motion should be smooth and purposeful: transitions between views, playback animations, and hover states should feel polished. Avoid: heavy borders, busy backgrounds, and any visual noise that competes with album artwork.
landing_page: Hero should showcase the listening experience — a curated playlist, featured artist, or new release with compelling artwork. Below the fold: key differentiators (catalog size, audio quality, exclusive content, free tier details). Plan comparison with transparent pricing. App store badges and cross-platform messaging. A sample player or preview functionality that lets visitors hear before committing. Social proof through user counts and curated editorial content. Avoid: generic music imagery, lengthy feature lists, and hiding the free tier.
dashboard_layout: The player is the persistent anchor — always visible at the bottom with track info, controls, progress, and queue access. Home view should lead with personalized recommendations: recently played, daily mixes, and new releases from followed artists. Library navigation should separate playlists, albums, artists, and podcasts. Search must be fast and support fuzzy matching across tracks, artists, albums, and lyrics. Browse section organized by genre, mood, and activity. Queue management with drag-to-reorder. Artist pages should showcase discography, related artists, and upcoming events. Avoid: burying the player, slow search, and recommendation algorithms that feel generic.
color_palette: Dark grey (not pure black) as the primary background — reduces eye strain during extended listening. Album art should dynamically influence ambient color accents where appropriate. Brand accent color for interactive elements (play buttons, active states, links). Use vibrant accent sparingly — it should draw the eye to actions, not decorate. Green or brand color for now-playing indicators. Text should be white or light grey with clear weight hierarchy. Avoid: competing with album art through heavy UI coloring, and light themes as default since dark mode is the established convention for music apps.
essential_ux: Playback reliability is the foundation — the player must never stutter, lose position, or fail silently. Transition between tracks should be gapless. Offline mode with download management is essential for mobile. Search speed must be near-instant. Queue and playlist management should support drag-and-drop and batch operations. Cross-device handoff (phone to desktop to speaker) should be seamless. Audio quality settings should be accessible but not overwhelming. Social features (sharing, collaborative playlists) should be discoverable but not intrusive. Accessibility: ensure all controls are keyboard-navigable and screen reader-compatible, with visible focus indicators against dark backgrounds.
ui_style_bias: Dark, immersive chrome; album-art-driven color, minimal UI borders, fluid transitions, persistent playback bar, and content-dense browsing

keywords: video, streaming, ott, movies, shows, series, watch, entertainment, tv, content platform
visual_style: Cinematic and immersive with dark-mode-first design. Content thumbnails and poster art should dominate every view — the UI exists to frame content, not compete with it. Typography should be bold for titles and light for metadata, creating clear hierarchy against dark backgrounds. Horizontal scrolling carousels are the established pattern for content rows. Motion should be purposeful: hover previews, smooth transitions, and loading states that do not break immersion. Avoid: bright UI chrome, heavy borders, and any design element that pulls attention from content imagery.
landing_page: Hero should be a full-bleed featured title with trailer auto-play (muted) and a prominent Watch Now or Start Free Trial CTA. Below: content carousels organized by genre, trending, and editorial picks. Plan comparison if applicable — keep it to 2-3 tiers. Device compatibility showcase. Content exclusives or originals section. Social proof through subscriber counts or critical acclaim. Avoid: lengthy copy, static heroes, visible content limitations, and pricing that feels complex.
dashboard_layout: Home screen is a content discovery engine — personalized rows (Continue Watching, Recommended, Trending, New Releases) with large horizontal thumbnails. Each thumbnail shows title, brief metadata, and match percentage or rating on hover. Content detail pages should include synopsis, cast, related titles, and season/episode navigation for series. Watchlist management. Profile switching with individual recommendation engines. Parental controls and content ratings clearly visible. Search with predictive suggestions and voice support. Avoid: text-heavy layouts, small thumbnails, and navigation that takes more than 2 clicks to reach any content.
color_palette: Near-black background as primary — this is a viewing environment, not a reading one. Brand accent color for CTAs and active navigation. Content metadata in light grey, not white, to avoid competing with thumbnails. Genre or category can have subtle color coding. Progress bars for partially watched content should be visually distinct. Avoid: any light theme, colored backgrounds behind content rows, and high-saturation UI elements that pull focus from poster art. Ensure sufficient contrast for UI controls against dark backgrounds.
essential_ux: Content discovery and playback quality are the two UX pillars. Video player must support adaptive bitrate, captions in multiple languages, picture-in-picture, and playback speed. Continue Watching must be accurate and prominent — nothing frustrates users more than losing their place. Thumbnail loading must be fast — empty carousels feel broken. Autoplay next episode with a skippable countdown. Search should understand natural language queries. Download for offline viewing is expected. Recommendations should improve over time and allow easy dismissal of uninteresting suggestions. Accessibility: audio descriptions for key content, comprehensive caption support, and keyboard navigation for all player controls.
ui_style_bias: Cinematic dark interface; poster-art-dominant layout, full-bleed hero, horizontal content rails, immersive hover previews, and minimal chrome

keywords: job board, recruitment, hiring, careers, talent, employment, job search, staffing, applicant, job listing
visual_style: Functional and scannable with a focus on content density done right. Typography should prioritize readability at small sizes for listing details while maintaining strong hierarchy for job titles and company names. Layouts should use consistent card or row patterns that support rapid scanning. Visual design should be restrained — the content is utilitarian, and the interface should make browsing efficient rather than decorative. Search and filtering are the primary interaction patterns and must be visually prominent. Avoid: heavy imagery, playful branding, and layouts that sacrifice scan-ability for visual interest.
landing_page: Hero should lead with a search bar — this is a utility-first product. Below the fold: featured jobs or trending categories, employer logos for social proof, and platform metrics (jobs posted, companies hiring, successful placements). For job seekers: clear paths to browse or upload a resume. For employers: a separate but accessible CTA for posting jobs. Pricing for employers should be transparent. Testimonials should come from both sides of the marketplace. Avoid: generic career imagery, hiding the search, and combining job-seeker and employer messaging in confusing ways.
dashboard_layout: Job seeker dashboard: saved jobs, application status tracker (applied, viewed, interviewing, offer), recommended jobs based on profile, and profile completion indicator. Employer dashboard: active postings with applicant counts, pipeline view for candidates (new, screening, interview, offer), and posting analytics. Both sides need strong search and filter: location, salary range, experience level, remote/hybrid, date posted. Job detail pages should show the essentials above the fold: title, company, location, salary range, and apply button. Avoid: requiring login to view job details, and hiding salary information.
color_palette: Professional blue as primary creates trust without feeling corporate. Success green for positive states (matched, hired, new listings). Neutral greys for backgrounds and card borders to let content dominate. Accent color for primary CTAs (Apply, Post Job). Avoid: vibrant or playful palettes that undermine professional credibility, dark themes as default (job browsing is a daytime activity for most users), and category color coding that creates visual noise across dense listings.
essential_ux: The core UX metric is time-to-relevant-result. Search must be fast, intelligent, and prominent on every page. Filtering should support boolean-style combinations without requiring technical knowledge. Job listings must be scannable — title, company, location, salary, and posted date visible without clicking. Application flow should be completable in under 3 minutes; support resume parsing and profile auto-fill. For employers: posting a job should take under 5 minutes. Mobile is critical — job seekers browse during commutes and breaks. Avoid: requiring account creation before browsing, and application flows that redirect to external career sites without warning.
ui_style_bias: Efficient, scan-friendly layout; professional blue palette, prominent search, dense but readable listings, clear status indicators, and utility-first design

keywords: marketplace, peer-to-peer, p2p, buy, sell, classifieds, listings, secondhand, resale, two-sided
visual_style: Trust-centered and content-dense. The visual framework must serve two audiences (buyers and sellers) without confusion. Product imagery should be prominent — large thumbnails with consistent aspect ratios. Typography should be functional and scannable for listings while supporting detailed product descriptions. Card-based layouts with clear price, condition, and seller information. The interface should feel safe and transparent. Avoid: visually heavy branding, inconsistent listing presentations, and layouts that make the marketplace feel disorganized or untrustworthy.
landing_page: Hero should immediately communicate what the marketplace offers and its trust proposition. Search bar is the primary interaction — make it dominant. Below the fold: popular categories with imagery, featured or trending listings, and platform trust signals (buyer protection, verification, transaction count). Dual CTAs: one for buyers (Browse/Search) and one for sellers (Start Selling), but do not split the hero. Social proof through transaction volume and user reviews. Avoid: cluttered category grids, auto-rotating carousels, and messaging that focuses on only one side of the marketplace.
dashboard_layout: Buyer view: browse and search with robust filtering (price, condition, location, category, seller rating). Listing cards show image, title, price, condition, seller rating, and shipping info. Product detail pages include multiple photos, description, seller profile, and similar items. Seller view: listing management with status (active, sold, drafts), messages from buyers, earnings/payout history, and performance metrics. Messaging system between buyer and seller with transaction context. Review and rating system visible on both profiles. Avoid: hiding seller information, requiring login to browse, and checkout flows that feel insecure.
color_palette: Neutral, trustworthy palette. White or light grey backgrounds let product imagery speak. Use a brand accent for primary CTAs (Buy, List Item). Green for verified/trusted states, amber for caution (new seller, no reviews). Avoid: heavy brand coloring that competes with product photos, dark themes for browsing (product photography needs accurate color rendering), and inconsistent color treatment across listing cards that makes the feed feel chaotic.
essential_ux: Trust is the existential UX challenge for P2P marketplaces. Buyer protection policies must be visible and clear. Seller verification badges reduce friction. Review systems should be prominent and honest — do not hide negative reviews. Payment should feel secure: escrow indicators, refund policies, and encrypted payment badges. Search and filtering must handle large catalogs efficiently. Listing creation for sellers should be fast: support photo upload from camera, auto-suggest categories, and price guidance. Mobile is primary for many P2P marketplaces — optimize for thumb-zone navigation and camera-first listing creation. Performance matters: image-heavy feeds must load progressively without layout shifts.
ui_style_bias: Trust-first marketplace; neutral backgrounds, prominent product imagery, clear seller signals, dual-audience navigation, and secure transaction cues

keywords: logistics, delivery, shipping, fleet, tracking, dispatch, courier, freight, supply chain, last mile
visual_style: Functional and operationally clear. The visual language should prioritize status communication and spatial orientation (maps, routes, timelines). Typography must be legible at small sizes for dense data tables and tracking details. Layouts should be grid-based with consistent card or row patterns for shipments and orders. Color is functional, not decorative — reserved for status indication. Avoid: playful branding, heavy illustration, and any visual treatment that slows comprehension of operational data.
landing_page: Hero should communicate the core service promise: speed, reliability, coverage area, or cost. A tracking input or quote calculator as the primary CTA drives immediate engagement. Below the fold: service tiers with clear comparison (same-day, next-day, freight), coverage map, and integration partners or API documentation for B2B audiences. Trust signals: on-time delivery rates, shipment volume, insurance coverage, and client logos. Testimonials should focus on reliability and problem resolution. Avoid: vague messaging, stock photos of trucks, and hiding pricing behind contact forms.
dashboard_layout: Real-time shipment tracking as the primary view: map with active deliveries, status timeline (picked up, in transit, out for delivery, delivered), and ETA with confidence indicator. Dashboard should surface exceptions and alerts prominently — late shipments, failed deliveries, and pending actions need immediate visibility. Fleet or driver management with status indicators. Analytics secondary: delivery performance, cost per shipment, on-time rates. Route optimization visualization where applicable. Avoid: burying exceptions in tables, stale data displays, and dashboards that require manual refresh.
color_palette: Blue as primary conveys reliability and professionalism. Use a traffic-light semantic system: green for delivered/on-time, amber for in-transit/delayed, red for failed/exception. Orange works well as a secondary accent for tracking and action states. Backgrounds should be light and clean for data density. Map overlays need high contrast against geographic backgrounds. Avoid: dark themes as default (operational dashboards need daytime readability), decorative color, and status colors that conflict with traffic-light conventions.
essential_ux: Real-time accuracy is the foundational UX requirement — stale tracking data destroys trust faster than anything else. Show delivery dates, not delivery speeds. Provide all tracking details on your own page rather than redirecting to carrier sites. Notifications should be proactive: notify before the user checks, not after. Mobile is critical for both end customers checking deliveries and drivers in the field. Offline capability matters for drivers in low-connectivity areas. Error states must be specific: which shipment, what went wrong, what to do next. API documentation (if B2B) should be clean, interactive, and well-versioned.
ui_style_bias: Operational clarity; status-driven color, map-centric tracking, real-time data prominence, exception-first alerts, and utility-dense layouts

keywords: agriculture, farm tech, farming, crop, agritech, soil, livestock, harvest, precision agriculture, agronomics
visual_style: Practical, clear, and designed for harsh conditions. Interfaces must be readable in direct sunlight — avoid low-contrast text and subtle UI elements. Typography should be large and bold with strong weight differentiation. Layouts should be simple with generous touch targets for gloved or calloused hands. Data visualizations (weather, soil, yield) should be immediately interpretable without legends or tooltips. Earthy, natural color palette that feels grounded rather than clinical. Avoid: dark themes (outdoor readability), thin typography, small interactive elements, and any design that assumes high digital literacy.
landing_page: Hero should communicate the specific farming problem solved: yield optimization, water management, livestock health, or market access. Use real agricultural photography, not generic stock. Below the fold: feature overview tied to tangible outcomes (bushels per acre, water savings, labor hours reduced). Pricing should be transparent and tied to farm size or usage. Testimonials from real farmers with farm names and locations. Demo or trial CTA should emphasize ease of setup. Avoid: tech jargon, abstract data visualizations on the landing page, and messaging that talks to investors rather than farmers.
dashboard_layout: Dashboard should surface weather and time-sensitive alerts first — frost warnings, irrigation schedules, pest alerts, and harvest windows. Map-based field overview with color-coded crop health indicators. Sensor data (soil moisture, temperature, humidity) displayed as simple gauges or trend lines, not complex charts. Task management for planting, spraying, and harvest schedules. Historical yield data for season-over-season comparison. Offline mode is mandatory — sync when connectivity returns. Navigation must be flat and obvious, ideally 3-5 primary sections. Avoid: deep navigation hierarchies, features that require constant connectivity, and data displays that need agricultural science knowledge to interpret.
color_palette: Earth tones as the foundation: deep greens, warm browns, and sky blues connect to the agricultural context. Use semantic colors for crop health (green for healthy, amber for stress, red for critical). Weather indicators should use intuitive color associations (blue for rain, orange for heat). Backgrounds must be light enough for outdoor screen readability. High contrast is non-negotiable — many users are older with reduced vision. Avoid: muted or pastel palettes that wash out in sunlight, dark backgrounds, and decorative color gradients that reduce data clarity.
essential_ux: Offline-first is the primary UX constraint — rural connectivity is unreliable and the app must function in the field without signal. Data sync should be automatic and conflict-free when connectivity returns. Touch targets must be minimum 48px for use with gloves. Interfaces should support users with low digital literacy: use icons with labels, avoid gesture-only interactions, and provide simple onboarding. Sensor data should surface actionable recommendations, not raw numbers. Localization matters: support local units (acres vs hectares), languages, and regional crop types. Performance must be optimized for older Android devices common in agricultural markets. Notifications should be timely and actionable — a frost alert after the frost is useless.
ui_style_bias: Rugged, sunlight-ready UI; earthy tones, large touch targets, sensor-driven dashboards, offline-capable, and plain-language data displays

keywords: construction, architecture, building, contractor, blueprint, project management, engineering, renovation, structural, general contractor
visual_style: Structured and precise with a material sensibility. Typography should be clean and technical — a strong sans-serif that communicates engineering confidence. Layouts should use clear grid systems that mirror the precision of architectural work. Photography and 3D renders should be large and high-resolution, given the visual nature of the work. Use ample whitespace to frame project imagery. The palette should be restrained and professional — let the work speak. Avoid: playful design, rounded elements, and anything that undermines the perception of technical competence and safety.
landing_page: Hero should feature a flagship project with striking photography or a 3D render. Lead with the firm's specialty (commercial, residential, renovation, infrastructure) and scale of work. Portfolio below the fold organized by project type with large thumbnails, project name, and scope. Services overview should be concise — not paragraph descriptions. Team section with credentials, certifications, and years of experience. Safety record and compliance certifications are trust signals unique to this industry. CTA should invite project consultation. Avoid: generic construction stock photos, cluttered project grids, and burying the portfolio below marketing copy.
dashboard_layout: If a project management portal exists, organize around active projects with timeline visualization (Gantt-style or milestone-based). Each project shows: phase status, upcoming milestones, budget vs. actual, and document library (blueprints, permits, change orders). Photo documentation of progress with date stamps. RFI and change order tracking with clear approval workflows. Team directory with role assignments per project. Subcontractor management where applicable. Avoid: overly complex dashboards — construction stakeholders want status clarity, not analytics depth.
color_palette: Neutral, professional palette: greys, charcoals, and whites as the foundation, reflecting materials like concrete and steel. A single strong accent (safety orange, blueprint blue, or architectural gold) for interactive elements and emphasis. Background should be clean white or very light grey to let project photography dominate. Avoid: multiple bright colors that feel consumer-grade, dark themes that reduce blueprint readability, and color choices that conflict with standard safety colors (orange, yellow, red) used in the industry.
essential_ux: The portfolio is the primary conversion driver — every UX decision should serve project presentation. Photography and renders must load fast despite high resolution; use progressive loading and optimized formats. Project filtering (by type, scale, location, completion date) helps visitors self-qualify. Mobile must work well — stakeholders review project sites on tablets and phones at job sites. Contact should be frictionless with minimal required fields. If a client portal exists, document management is critical: version control, approval workflows, and secure sharing of sensitive blueprints and contracts. Accessibility (WCAG AA) is important for compliance-conscious firms.
ui_style_bias: Precise, material-inspired design; grid-structured layouts, technical typography, project-showcase hierarchy, safety-color accents, and blueprint-grade clarity

keywords: automotive, car dealership, vehicles, auto, dealer, cars, automobile, showroom, inventory, test drive
visual_style: High-impact and immersive with a focus on vehicle presentation. Photography must be large, detailed, and professionally lit — vehicles are visual products and every pixel of imagery matters. Typography should be bold for model names and pricing, clean for specifications. Layouts should support both browsing (grid inventory) and deep-dive (vehicle detail pages). Interactive elements (360-degree views, color configurators) should feel responsive and premium. The experience should build excitement while maintaining trust. Avoid: cluttered inventory displays, low-quality photos, aggressive pop-ups, and anything that feels like a high-pressure sales floor.
landing_page: Hero should showcase a flagship or high-demand vehicle with full-bleed imagery and a clear CTA (Browse Inventory, Book a Test Drive). Below the fold: featured vehicles or categories (new, used, certified pre-owned), search/filter entry point, and current promotions or financing offers. Trust signals: manufacturer certifications, customer reviews, years in business, and warranty information. Financing calculator or pre-qualification CTA for price-sensitive visitors. Avoid: rotating banners with competing offers, auto-playing music, excessive pop-ups for chat or trade-in, and hiding inventory behind forms.
dashboard_layout: Inventory management is the core dashboard for dealers: vehicle listings with status (available, reserved, sold), days on lot, pricing, and lead source. Lead management pipeline: new inquiries, test drives scheduled, negotiations, and closed deals. Sales performance metrics and team leaderboard. Service department scheduling and history. For consumer-facing apps: saved vehicles, comparison tools, financing status, and service appointment booking. Avoid: cramming all dealer operations into one view — use role-based dashboards (sales, service, management).
color_palette: Dark backgrounds can create a premium showroom feel for vehicle showcase pages. Brand-aligned accent colors for CTAs and interactive elements. White or light grey for inventory listing backgrounds where scan-ability matters. Use red or brand color for pricing and offers — these are high-attention elements. Vehicle color swatches should be accurate to real paint colors. Avoid: palettes that compete with vehicle photography, overly colorful UI that feels consumer-grade, and inconsistent color treatment between new and used inventory.
essential_ux: The core UX metric is time-to-relevant-vehicle — users decide within seconds whether your inventory matches their needs. Search and filtering must be fast and support: make, model, year, price range, mileage, body type, and features. Vehicle detail pages should show all key information above the fold: price, mileage, key specs, and multiple photos. Photo galleries must support swiping and zooming. Financing calculators should be transparent and pre-fillable. Test drive booking should take under 60 seconds. Mobile is critical — most car shopping begins on phones. Page performance matters enormously for image-heavy inventory pages; use lazy loading. Avoid: requiring account creation to see pricing, and chat pop-ups that obscure vehicle imagery.
ui_style_bias: Showroom-quality presentation; bold vehicle imagery, dark premium backdrops, fast inventory filtering, configurator-ready interactions, and trust-forward pricing

keywords: photography, studio, photographer, photo, portraits, events, shoots, visual, gallery, sessions
visual_style: Minimal and image-dominant. The interface must serve as a frame for the work — every design decision should enhance photography, not compete with it. Typography should be elegant and restrained: a clean serif or minimal sans-serif for navigation and captions. Layouts should use generous whitespace with full-bleed or near-full-bleed imagery. Backgrounds should be neutral (white, near-black, or warm grey) to allow photographs to set the color tone. Grid systems should be flexible to accommodate both landscape and portrait orientations. Avoid: busy backgrounds, heavy branding, colorful UI elements, and any chrome that distracts from the photographs.
landing_page: Open with the strongest work — a full-bleed hero image or a curated slideshow of 3-5 best shots. Minimal text overlay; let the photography make the first impression. Below the fold: portfolio organized by category (weddings, portraits, commercial, events) with consistent thumbnail sizing. Brief about section that communicates style and personality. Packages or pricing information (even starting-from ranges) reduce inquiry friction. Client testimonials with event type context. Contact/booking CTA that is always accessible but visually unobtrusive. Avoid: text-heavy hero sections, generic stock photography on a photographer's site, and hiding the portfolio behind navigation.
dashboard_layout: Most photography studios do not need a dashboard. If a client gallery or proofing portal exists, organize around the session or event. Display images in a clean masonry or grid layout with download, favorite, and print-order functionality. Password protection per gallery for client privacy. About section with the bakers story, sourcing philosophy, or founding narrative. Catering or custom cake information for high-value orders. Instagram feed or gallery showing daily specials and behind-the-scenes baking. Customer reviews. Avoid: PDF menus, menus without photos, and hiding location and hours below the fold.
dashboard_layout: Most bakeries do not need a customer-facing dashboard. If online ordering exists, provide: order status with estimated ready time, order history with reorder functionality, loyalty or rewards tracking, and saved favorites. For the business side: daily order queue organized by pickup time, custom cake requests with specifications and timeline, inventory tracking for perishables, and daily production planning. The ordering interface should support both advance ordering and same-day pickup. Avoid: complex checkout flows for simple counter purchases.
color_palette: Warm, appetite-stimulating palette: cream, warm brown, honey gold, and soft butter tones as the foundation. These colors evoke baking ingredients and warmth. A single stronger accent for CTAs (warm coral, brick red, or deep teal). Photography provides the color richness — the UI palette should be a warm, neutral frame. Backgrounds should be warm cream or soft white, never stark white. Avoid: cool blues and greys that suppress appetite, dark backgrounds that make food look unappetizing, and saturated colors that compete with food photography.
essential_ux: Online ordering convenience is the primary differentiator for bakeries with web presence — reduce phone calls and increase order accuracy. Menu presentation must include photos for at least the top sellers; menus without images underperform. Location, hours, and phone number must be findable within 2 seconds. Mobile is the primary browsing channel, especially for local searches. Page speed matters for local SEO rankings. Special orders (custom cakes, catering) need a dedicated flow with enough detail to quote accurately: size, flavor, design, date, delivery or pickup. Daily specials or seasonal items should be easy to update without redesigning the page. Avoid: PDF-only menus that frustrate mobile users, and websites that cannot answer the three basic questions immediately: what do you sell, where are you, and when are you open.
ui_style_bias: Warm, appetite-forward design; bakery-toned palette, hero food photography, prominent hours and location, simple ordering flow, and artisanal personality

keywords: coffee, coffee shop, cafe, espresso, roastery, barista, coffeehouse, latte, roaster, brew
visual_style: Warm, intimate, and craft-conscious. The visual language should evoke the sensory experience of coffee — warmth, aroma, ritual. Typography should be distinctive but readable: a characterful display font for the brand paired with a clean, warm body font. Photography should be rich and atmospheric: close-ups of latte art, beans, brewing processes, and the interior space. Layouts should be simple and inviting. The experience should feel like the cafe itself: unhurried, personal, and detail-oriented. Avoid: corporate chain aesthetics, generic coffee stock photography, cluttered layouts, and cold or clinical design.
landing_page: Hero should feature atmospheric photography of the space or a signature drink, with location and hours immediately visible. Menu CTA or mobile ordering link if available. Below the fold: the menu organized simply (espresso, filter, seasonal, food, retail beans). Origin story or sourcing philosophy — single-origin or specialty coffee customers care deeply about provenance. Retail section if beans or merchandise are sold online. Loyalty program promotion. Location with parking and transit details. Events or community involvement (cuppings, live music). Avoid: hiding the menu, overcomplicating the experience for what should be a simple local business site, and failing to show the actual interior space.
dashboard_layout: Most coffee shops do not need a customer-facing dashboard. If mobile ordering exists: simple order builder with size, milk, and modifier selections. Order status with estimated ready time. Order history with one-tap reorder for regulars. Loyalty points or stamp card tracking. Saved favorites. Subscription management for bean deliveries if applicable. For the business side: real-time order queue, inventory alerts for running low, and daily sales summary. Avoid: over-engineering — coffee ordering should be faster than standing in line, not slower.
color_palette: Rich, warm coffee-inspired palette: deep espresso brown, warm cream, coffee-with-milk caramel, and raw linen tones. These create an immediate sensory association. A single accent color for CTAs and highlights (warm terracotta, sage green, or muted gold). Photography should carry the visual richness. Backgrounds should be warm cream or soft parchment, evoking paper and natural materials. Avoid: stark whites that feel cold, saturated colors that overpower the warm coffee aesthetic, dark backgrounds for the main site (reserve dark for evening events or retail sections), and any color that does not feel handcrafted.
essential_ux: The website exists primarily to answer four questions: where are you, when are you open, what do you serve, and can I order ahead. Answer all four within 5 seconds of landing. Location and hours must be visible without scrolling. Mobile ordering (if offered) is the highest-value feature — ensure it is faster than ordering in person. The origin story and sourcing details build emotional connection and justify premium pricing for specialty shops. Retail bean sales and subscriptions are the highest-margin digital channel — make them prominent without overwhelming the cafe experience. Photography must be authentic to the actual space — visitors will feel deceived if the website atmosphere does not match the shop. Local SEO (Google Business integration, location keywords) drives the majority of traffic for independent coffee shops.
ui_style_bias: Cozy craft aesthetic; espresso-toned palette, atmospheric photography, simple menu-forward layout, warm textures, and origin-story warmth

keywords: brewery, winery, craft beer, wine, taproom, tasting room, vineyard, microbrewery, cellar, vintner
visual_style: Rich, artisanal, and story-driven. The visual language should communicate craft, heritage, and sensory experience. Typography should have character — a distinctive display font that reflects the brand personality (rustic, modern craft, or refined) paired with a readable body font. Photography should be atmospheric: the production space, ingredients, pours, and the people behind the product. Layouts should balance storytelling with e-commerce functionality. Dark backgrounds can work for evening/tasting atmosphere, but product pages need accurate color rendering. Avoid: generic stock imagery, corporate beverage branding, and designs that feel more like a liquor store than a craft producer.
landing_page: Hero should establish the brand atmosphere — a full-bleed image of the tasting room, vineyard, or brewing process with a compelling tagline. Below the fold: default to showing all products rather than categories — for under 15 products, no filtering is needed. Product cards with bottle shot (hover to reveal lifestyle imagery), name, variety, and price. Tasting room or taproom information with hours, reservation link, and location. Events calendar (tastings, releases, food pairings). The story section: founders, process, terroir, or ingredients — this content drives emotional purchase decisions. Club or membership promotion. Avoid: confusing navigation that buries tasting room info, weak CTAs, and product pages that do not help customers distinguish between similar offerings.
dashboard_layout: If a club/membership portal exists: upcoming shipments with contents and delivery date, membership tier and benefits, order history, account management, and event access. For the tasting room: reservation management and waitlist. For the business side: inventory by batch, taplist management with real-time status (on tap, running low, kicked), production schedule, and club member analytics. Menu or taplist must be easy to update since rotating selections are expected. Avoid: static menus that do not reflect current availability, and club management that requires phone calls for basic changes.
color_palette: Product-appropriate palette: amber, deep gold, and rich brown tones for breweries; burgundy, deep purple, and aged gold for wineries. Dark backgrounds can create atmospheric product showcases, but product photography needs accurate color rendering (especially for wine label readability). Cream or warm white for text-heavy and e-commerce sections. Metallic accents (gold, copper, brass) add craft premium feel. Avoid: bright or neon colors that feel mass-market, clinical whites that strip the artisanal atmosphere, and UI colors that interfere with accurate perception of beverage color in product photos.
essential_ux: The website must bridge the physical experience gap — without taste and smell, storytelling and photography carry the entire sensory load. Product differentiation is critical: when multiple offerings look similar (e.g., three IPAs or four Chardonnays), use callouts for body type, flavor profile, or production method. Critic reviews outperform user reviews for small producers — cite the reviewer. Product detail pages should structure information in scannable sections: tasting notes, food pairings, production details, awards. 65-75% of traffic is mobile; optimize accordingly. Tasting room reservations should be bookable online. E-commerce checkout must handle shipping compliance (age verification, state restrictions). Menu or taplist must be trivially updateable for rotating selections. Avoid: outdated menus that do not reflect what is actually available, and product pages that make all offerings look identical.
ui_style_bias: Rich, craft-story-driven design; atmospheric photography, artisanal typography, amber-to-burgundy palette, rotating menu integration, and tasting-room-to-web bridge

keywords: airline, aviation, flights, air travel, booking, carrier, air, flying, airways, ticketing
visual_style: Efficient, trustworthy, and globally polished. The design must handle extreme information density (dates, routes, prices, classes, ancillaries) without overwhelming users. Typography must be precise and legible at small sizes for fare comparisons and flight details. Layouts should be highly structured with clear visual hierarchy separating search, results, and booking steps. The interface should communicate competence and reliability — travelers trust airlines that feel organized. Support for multiple languages and currencies is foundational. Avoid: decorative design that slows comprehension, cluttered fare displays, dark themes for the booking flow, and playful branding that undermines the gravity of air travel.
landing_page: Hero should be a prominent flight search widget: origin, destination, dates, passenger count, and class. This is the only element that matters above the fold. Below the fold: promotional fares or route deals with specific prices, loyalty program promotion, and route map or destination inspiration for leisure travelers. Trust signals: safety record, fleet information, and alliance memberships. App download promotion with mobile-specific features (boarding pass, real-time updates). Status or flight tracking for existing travelers. Avoid: hero imagery that pushes the search below the fold, hiding promotional fares, and mixing business and leisure messaging in confusing ways.
dashboard_layout: Booking management as the primary authenticated view: upcoming trips with itinerary, booking reference, seat selection, and check-in status. Trip timeline showing each leg with departure, arrival, gate, and terminal. Boarding pass access (mobile and printable). Loyalty program status: points balance, tier progress, and redemption options. Flight status with real-time updates and delay notifications. Past trips for rebooking. Baggage tracking. Ancillary management (seat upgrades, meals, lounge access). Avoid: booking flows that take more than 5 steps, hiding the total price until the final step, and ancillary upsell screens that prevent users from advancing without explicit action.
color_palette: Brand-centric palette: airline identity color as primary (this is one of few product types where brand color supersedes UX convention). Sky blue or white as secondary for the booking flow — clean and trustworthy. Price displays should use high contrast against neutral backgrounds for easy scanning. Semantic colors: green for confirmed/available, amber for limited/warning, red for unavailable/cancelled. Fare class differentiation through subtle background tinting or border color. Avoid: dark backgrounds for search results and fare comparison (readability is critical), color coding that varies between mobile and desktop, and decorative color that competes with pricing information.
essential_ux: The booking flow is the entire product — optimize relentlessly for completion rate. Search results must load fast and display clearly: price, times, duration, stops, and aircraft. A persistent price summary must be visible throughout the multi-step booking process so users always know the running total. Ancillary upsells (seats, bags, meals) must be clearly optional and never block progression. Fare comparison should be honest: show total price including mandatory fees, not base fare. Mobile is the primary channel for check-in, boarding pass, and flight status — these must be flawless. Push notifications for gate changes, delays, and boarding should be real-time and reliable. Multi-language and multi-currency support must be seamless, not bolted-on. Accessibility (WCAG AA) is critical for a public transportation service. Avoid: dark patterns that trick users into purchasing unwanted ancillaries, and booking flows that lose state on back-button navigation.
ui_style_bias: Globally polished efficiency; brand-centric palette, search-dominant hero, persistent price summary, structured fare comparison, and flight-status-forward mobile experience

keywords: news, media, journalism, press, publication, editorial, current events, reporting, headlines, newsroom
visual_style: Content-first with unwavering readability. Typography is the design — invest heavily in a typographic system that handles headlines, body text, captions, bylines, and pullquotes with clear hierarchy. Serif fonts for body text improve long-form readability; bold sans-serifs work well for headlines. Layouts should support rapid scanning of headlines while providing comfortable long-form reading. Information density should be high on the homepage and section pages, low on article pages. Whitespace around article text is essential for reading comfort. Avoid: decorative design that competes with content, distracting sidebar widgets, autoplay video on article pages, and typography that sacrifices readability for personality.
landing_page: Homepage is a news product — it should surface the most important and most recent stories with clear editorial hierarchy: lead story with large imagery, secondary stories in a grid, and section teasers. Breaking news banner capability. Category/section navigation must be fast and predictable. Below the fold: section previews (politics, business, culture, opinion) with 3-5 story teasers each. Newsletter signup CTA. Subscription or membership promotion that communicates the value of journalism without being obtrusive. Avoid: auto-rotating carousels that obscure editorial judgment, cluttered homepages where everything competes for attention, and hero layouts that bury breaking news capability.
dashboard_layout: For editorial teams: CMS-driven publishing workflow, analytics per article (views, read depth, shares), topic and author performance tracking, and SEO optimization suggestions. For subscribers: saved articles, reading history, newsletter preferences, and subscription management. For all users: article reading experience should include: adjustable text size, estimated read time, progress indicator for long pieces, related articles, and social sharing. Avoid: dashboards that prioritize vanity metrics over audience insight, and reader-facing features that interrupt the reading experience.
color_palette: Brand identity palette: most news organizations have established colors — these should be used for navigation and brand elements. Article pages should be typographically neutral: near-black text on warm or neutral white, with minimal color interference. Category or section color coding can aid navigation but must be subtle. Link colors should be clearly distinguished from body text. Breaking news indicators in red or high-contrast accent. Avoid: dark themes as default for reading (reduces perceived neutrality and readability), colored backgrounds behind article text, and UI colors that create visual fatigue during extended reading sessions.
essential_ux: Article format and presentation clarity is the single biggest driver of user satisfaction — a one-point improvement in format satisfaction raises overall UX quality by 12%. Reading experience must be optimized: 55-75 character line length, generous line height (1.5-1.6x), clear heading hierarchy, and no interstitial ads that break reading flow. Homepage must load fast and update frequently for breaking news. Paywall implementation should be clear and fair — metered paywalls outperform hard walls for acquisition. Search must span the full archive with relevant, date-aware results. Mobile reading must be equal to desktop — most news consumption happens on phones. Push notifications for breaking news must be timely, relevant, and not overused. Accessibility (WCAG AA) is essential for a public information service. Performance is critical: every 100ms of load time correlates with reduced engagement for news sites.
ui_style_bias: Typography-led editorial clarity; reading-optimized line length, neutral article pages, dense-but-scannable homepage, breaking-news-ready hierarchy, and subscription-respectful paywall

keywords: magazine, blog, editorial, articles, content, publishing, writer, columnist, opinion, digital magazine
visual_style: Typography-driven and editorially refined. This is a reading product — every design decision should serve comprehension and engagement with long-form content. Invest in a typographic system: serif body text for readability, bold sans-serif headlines for impact, and clear hierarchy across subheads, captions, bylines, and pullquotes. Layouts should balance visual richness (hero imagery, pullquotes, featured graphics) with comfortable reading zones. Whitespace around article body text is non-negotiable. Avoid: cluttered sidebars that compete with content, autoplay media, decorative UI elements that distract from reading, and typography that sacrifices legibility for personality.
landing_page: Homepage should present a curated editorial hierarchy: lead story with large imagery and compelling headline, secondary story grid, and section teasers. Category navigation (culture, tech, opinion, lifestyle) should be prominent and fast. Featured or editors-pick section adds editorial voice. Newsletter signup CTA integrated naturally, not as a popup. Author pages with bio, photo, and article archive. Below the fold: trending or most-read articles, category previews with 3-5 story teasers each. Subscription or membership promotion if applicable — focus on the value of the editorial voice, not generic access. Avoid: auto-rotating carousels, clickbait headlines, and homepage layouts that flatten all content to equal weight.
dashboard_layout: For editors: content calendar, draft management, SEO optimization suggestions, and per-article analytics (views, read depth, shares, time on page). For readers: saved articles, reading history, newsletter preferences, dark mode toggle, and subscription management. Article reading experience: estimated read time, progress indicator for long pieces, adjustable text size, related articles at the end, and social sharing. Comment system (if enabled) should be moderated and threaded. Avoid: analytics dashboards that prioritize page views over engagement depth, and reader features that interrupt the reading flow.
color_palette: Brand-forward palette for navigation and identity elements, but article pages should be typographically neutral. Near-black text on warm or neutral white for body text — never grey text on white. Category color coding can aid navigation but must be subtle and never bleed into article backgrounds. Link colors clearly distinguished from body text. Accent color for CTAs (subscribe, newsletter). Dark mode option with proper contrast ratios (not just inverted colors). Avoid: colored backgrounds behind article text (kills readability), high-saturation UI that causes fatigue during extended reading, and palettes that override editorial photography.
essential_ux: Reading experience quality is the core UX metric. Optimize line length (55-75 characters), line height (1.5-1.6x), and body text size (minimum 18px) for sustained reading comfort. Good editorial design makes readers forget they are on a screen. Article pages should minimize distractions: no autoplay video, no interstitial ads that break flow, and no sticky elements that reduce reading area. Page speed is critical — slow-loading articles lose readers before the first paragraph. Mobile reading must match desktop quality; most editorial consumption happens on phones. Search must span the full archive with relevant, date-aware results. Newsletter signup should offer genuine editorial value, not just access. Accessibility: proper heading hierarchy, alt text for editorial images, and screen reader compatibility for article structure.
ui_style_bias: Editorial craft meets digital clarity; typography-led hierarchy, reading-optimized body text, rich editorial imagery, neutral article backgrounds, and content-first density

keywords: freelancer, freelance, gig, independent contractor, self-employed, remote work, talent marketplace, skilled professional, project-based, contract work
visual_style: Professional and efficient with clear dual-audience design. The interface must serve both freelancers (selling skills) and clients (buying outcomes) without confusing either side. Typography should be clean and scannable — profile browsing requires rapid comparison. Layouts should use consistent card patterns for freelancer profiles with key information visible at a glance. Search and filtering are the primary interactions and must be prominent. The design should feel trustworthy and competent. Avoid: overly casual or startup-playful branding, inconsistent profile presentations, and layouts that blur the line between freelancer and client experiences.
landing_page: Hero should serve both audiences with a clear value proposition and separate entry paths: Find Talent and Find Work. Search bar with skill/category input as the primary CTA. Below the fold: popular categories with representative work samples, featured freelancers or projects, and platform metrics (projects completed, freelancers available, total paid out). Trust signals: payment protection, dispute resolution, and platform review scores. How-it-works section for new users (both sides). Testimonials from both freelancers and clients. Avoid: messaging that only speaks to one side of the marketplace, hiding the search, and generic gig economy imagery.
dashboard_layout: Freelancer dashboard: profile completeness indicator (drives matching quality), active proposals and their status, current projects with milestones and deadlines, earnings with payout schedule, reviews and ratings, and skill endorsements. Client dashboard: active projects with freelancer status, posted jobs with applicant counts, hiring pipeline, spend history, and saved freelancers. Both: messaging system with project context, file sharing, and time tracking where applicable. Search with robust filtering: skill, rate range, experience level, availability, location, and rating. Avoid: hiding earnings data from freelancers, and notification overload that does not distinguish urgent from routine.
color_palette: Professional, trust-building palette. Blue as primary conveys reliability for a financial transaction platform. Green for success states (project completed, payment sent, available). Neutral greys for backgrounds and card borders so portfolio work and profile photos dominate. Accent color for primary CTAs (Hire, Submit Proposal). Category colors can be used sparingly for skill area differentiation. Avoid: playful palettes that undermine professional credibility, dark themes as default (profile browsing is a daytime activity), and heavy brand coloring that competes with portfolio imagery.
essential_ux: Profile completeness is the #1 lever for matching quality — incentivize and guide freelancers to complete profiles through progress indicators and clear prompts. Search must be fast, intelligent, and support both keyword and category-based discovery. Profile cards should show: name, title, rating, hourly rate, skills, and a portfolio thumbnail without clicking. Proposal submission should be fast but structured — templates with customizable sections. Payment flow must feel secure: escrow indicators, milestone-based releases, and clear fee transparency. Mobile is important for messaging and notifications but desktop dominates for hiring and proposal work. Review systems must be bilateral (client reviews freelancer AND freelancer reviews client) to build marketplace trust. Avoid: requiring account creation before browsing, and payment flows that feel opaque about platform fees.
ui_style_bias: Professional dual-audience layout; trust-blue palette, scannable profile cards, robust search and filtering, portfolio-forward profiles, and secure transaction indicators

keywords: consulting, consultancy, advisory, management consulting, strategy, professional services, business consulting, consultant, advisory firm, strategic consulting
visual_style: Authoritative, polished, and substance-driven. The visual language should communicate intellectual rigor and business impact without feeling stuffy. Typography should be refined and professional — a strong serif or premium sans-serif that conveys expertise. Layouts should be clean and spacious with deliberate use of whitespace to signal premium positioning. Photography should show real team members in authentic settings — boardrooms and workshops, not stock handshakes. The overall tone should say: we think deeply and deliver results. Avoid: generic corporate design, busy layouts, stock business photography, and visual patterns borrowed from SaaS or startups.
landing_page: Hero should lead with the firm's core expertise and a results-oriented value proposition — not what you do, but what clients achieve. Below the fold: service areas or practice groups with concise descriptions. Case studies section is the most important content on the site — each should show client context, approach, and quantified outcome. Team section with senior leadership photos, credentials, and areas of expertise. Thought leadership section (articles, whitepapers, reports) that demonstrates domain knowledge. Industry or client logos for social proof. CTA should be Schedule a Consultation or Contact Us — never Get Started. Avoid: feature-benefit grids, pricing pages (consulting is custom-scoped), and generic messaging that could apply to any firm.
dashboard_layout: Most consulting firms do not need a client-facing dashboard. If a client portal exists, organize around: active engagements with deliverable timelines and status, document repository for shared materials (presentations, reports, data), meeting notes and action items, and invoice/billing summary. For internal use: pipeline management for new opportunities, resource allocation across engagements, utilization tracking, and knowledge management for reusable frameworks. Avoid: complex dashboards — consulting clients want deliverable status and document access, not analytics.
color_palette: Restrained, premium palette. Navy or charcoal as primary — conveys authority and seriousness. Gold, brass, or warm accent for subtle emphasis (CTAs, section dividers, headings). White or very light warm grey backgrounds for content areas. Photography and case study imagery provide visual interest — the UI palette should be a neutral frame. Limit to 3 colors maximum. Avoid: bright blues that feel tech-startup, trendy gradients, colorful UI elements that reduce perceived gravitas, and dark themes that feel more tech-company than professional services.
essential_ux: Case studies with quantified outcomes are the single most important content asset — invest heavily in their quality and presentation. Thought leadership content (articles, reports) drives organic traffic and establishes expertise; make it easy to find and share. Team profiles are high-traffic pages — credentials, experience, and a genuine photo build trust. Navigation should be shallow and predictable: services, industries, case studies, team, insights, contact. Mobile must work well for executive audiences who browse during commutes. Page speed matters for SEO and first impressions. Contact forms should be short (name, company, topic, message) and clearly indicate what happens next. Avoid: gated content that requires forms before any value is shown, and websites that talk about the firm's process more than client outcomes.
ui_style_bias: Authoritative premium restraint; navy-gold palette, case-study-forward content, refined typography, whitespace-rich layouts, and substance-over-style hierarchy

keywords: marketing agency, advertising, digital marketing, creative agency, brand agency, media agency, campaign, ad agency, growth agency, performance marketing
visual_style: Bold, results-driven, and creatively confident. The site is a portfolio piece — the design itself demonstrates capability. Typography should be large and expressive for headlines, clean for body text. Layouts can break conventions intentionally — asymmetric grids, bold section transitions, and unexpected interactions demonstrate creative range. Motion and animation should feel crafted and purposeful. Photography and case study imagery should be rich and full-bleed. The overall tone should communicate both creative excellence and measurable business impact. Avoid: safe corporate design, templated layouts, stock photography, and visual restraint that contradicts the creative positioning.
landing_page: Hero should make an immediate creative impact — bold typography, striking imagery, or motion that demonstrates the agency's aesthetic point of view. Below the fold: case studies are the primary content. Each should lead with results (revenue growth, conversion lift, brand metrics) and show the creative work. Services section organized by capability (brand, digital, media, performance, content). Client logos for credibility. Team or culture section that shows personality. Awards and recognition. Contact CTA should feel like the beginning of a creative partnership, not a sales funnel. Avoid: lengthy service descriptions, generic hero messaging, and portfolio presentations that do not connect creative work to business outcomes.
dashboard_layout: Most marketing agencies do not need a client-facing dashboard. If a reporting portal exists: campaign performance dashboards with key metrics (ROAS, CPA, conversion rate, impressions), channel breakdowns, and trend lines. Content calendar with approval workflows. Asset library for approved creative. Invoice and contract management. For internal use: project management with deliverable tracking, resource allocation, and profitability per client. Avoid: dumping raw analytics without context — every metric should be paired with interpretation and next steps.
color_palette: Brand-expressive palette — marketing agencies have more creative freedom with color than most product types. Bold, distinctive color choices that differentiate from competitors. Dark backgrounds can create drama for case study presentations. High-contrast CTAs. The palette should feel intentional and ownable — if a competitor could use the same colors without noticing, it is not distinctive enough. Avoid: safe corporate blue-grey, inconsistent color usage that feels unplanned rather than bold, and palettes that compete with case study imagery rather than framing it.
essential_ux: The portfolio IS the pitch — case study quality is the single highest-impact investment. Each case study should show: the challenge, the creative solution, and the measurable result. Present creative work large and beautifully rendered. Page performance must be fast despite heavy imagery — use progressive loading and modern formats. Mobile must showcase work effectively; many prospects share agency links on phones. Contact should be frictionless — a short form or even just an email link. Agency sites often over-invest in about/culture pages and under-invest in case study depth; reverse this priority. Awards and recognition add credibility but should not dominate navigation. Avoid: case studies that show creative work without business outcomes, and sites that look like every other agency site.
ui_style_bias: Bold, results-forward creative; expressive typography, full-bleed case studies, distinctive color system, motion-rich interactions, and measurable-impact narrative

keywords: conference, webinar, virtual event, summit, symposium, seminar, online event, live stream, professional event, event platform
visual_style: Structured, professional, and information-rich. The interface must handle complex event information (multiple tracks, speakers, schedules, time zones) without overwhelming attendees. Typography should be clean and hierarchical — event names, session titles, speaker names, and time slots all need distinct treatment. Layouts should organize dense information into scannable patterns. The design should feel polished and current — event platforms reflect on the organizer's brand. Support for both live and on-demand content is essential. Avoid: cluttered agendas, poor time zone handling, playful design that undermines professional events, and layouts that make multi-day events hard to navigate.
landing_page: Hero should feature the event name, dates, and a compelling value proposition or keynote speaker highlight. Registration CTA must be the dominant action — large, high-contrast, and above the fold. Below the fold: agenda overview or track highlights, featured speakers with photos and credentials, sponsor logos, and early-bird or pricing tiers. Countdown timer creates urgency. Past event highlights or testimonials for recurring events. Virtual platform preview to set expectations for the experience. Networking or community features as a differentiator. Avoid: hiding the agenda behind registration, burying speaker information, and registration forms that ask for too much before showing value.
dashboard_layout: Four core components: registration, streaming sessions, engagement tools, and analytics. Attendee view: personalized agenda builder, session schedule with track filtering and time zone conversion, speaker profiles, live session access with Q&A and chat, networking directory, and on-demand replay library. Organizer view: registration analytics, session attendance tracking, engagement metrics, sponsor ROI reporting, and attendee feedback. Session experience: video player with slides sync, live Q&A queue, polls, and chat. Avoid: session navigation that loses context, chat that overwhelms the content, and replay access that is harder to find than live sessions.
color_palette: Professional, event-brand-flexible palette. The platform should support custom event branding (colors, logos) while maintaining usability. Default palette: professional blue with clean whites and neutral greys. Session tracks can use color coding for quick identification. Live indicators in red or pulsing accent. CTA buttons (Register, Join Session) in high-contrast treatment. Avoid: platform brand colors that override event branding, dark themes for daytime professional events, and color coding systems that use more than 6 track colors (becomes meaningless).
essential_ux: Registration completion rate is the primary conversion metric. Registration forms should collect only essential information upfront — name, email, and ticket type. Additional data (company, role, interests) can be collected post-registration or progressively. Time zone handling is critical: display all times in the attendee's local zone with a visible zone indicator. Agenda should be filterable by track, day, speaker, and topic. Networking features should reduce the cold-start problem: suggest connections based on shared interests or sessions. Mobile experience must support session access, agenda, and networking on the go. Push notifications for session reminders and schedule changes. Accessibility: live captions for sessions, keyboard navigation, and screen reader support for the full experience. Avoid: registration flows that require 10+ fields, and replay access that expires before attendees can watch.
ui_style_bias: Structured event clarity; professional palette, registration-dominant hero, filterable multi-track agenda, time-zone-aware scheduling, and seamless live-to-replay transition

keywords: membership, community, members, subscription, exclusive, club, forum, private community, member portal, paid community

Layouts should make browsing, searching, and contributing equally intuitive. The logged-in experience should feel distinctly different from the public marketing site. Community features (forums, comments, reactions) should encourage interaction without requiring effort.
