dashboard_layout: Gallery view as the primary interface: fluid masonry layout with varying artwork dimensions preserved, lazy-loaded high-resolution images with blur-up placeholders, and creator attribution overlaid on hover without obscuring the work. Collection pages group algorithmic variations with the ability to view generation parameters and transaction hashes. Creator profiles emphasize their generative systems and creative code rather than biographical narrative. Minting interface must be streamlined: preview the unique output being generated, show real-time gas estimates and total cost before commitment, and display transaction confirmation with immediate wallet delivery. Discovery flows use visual filtering by aesthetic characteristics, not just categorical tags — users should browse by color palette, complexity, or algorithmic approach. Provenance tracking shows full ownership history, resale activity, and royalty distribution. Secondary market integration for resales with creator royalties enforced by smart contract. Avoid: grid layouts that force artwork into uniform aspect ratios, minting flows that require multiple page transitions, and gallery views where platform UI competes visually with the artwork.
color_palette: Neutral canvas palette that defers to user-generated content. Deep charcoal or true black backgrounds as default to make artwork colors saturate and pop without interface interference. UI elements in subtle grays with minimal saturation — navigation, buttons, and metadata displays should be legible but visually recessive. Accent color for interactive elements should be a single high-contrast hue used sparingly for CTAs and minting actions. Generative artwork is the only source of vibrant color in the interface — the platform's palette must never compete. Status indicators for minting, transaction confirmation, and blockchain activity use semantic colors: green for confirmed, amber for pending, red for failed transactions. Avoid: colorful branding that fights with artwork, light-mode defaults that flatten generative color vibrancy, and rainbow UI palettes that create visual noise around the content.
essential_ux: Performance is the core UX constraint — slow image loading destroys the gallery browsing experience and creator credibility. Implement image CDN delivery, WebP with fallbacks, and lazy loading with IntersectionObserver for every gallery view. Creator attribution is non-negotiable and must persist across all contexts — artwork should never appear without visible credit to the generating artist. Minting flow is the monetization bottleneck: streamline to preview, confirm cost, and execute transaction in under three taps with no page reloads. Gas fee transparency prevents minting abandonment — show real-time estimates and allow users to adjust transaction speed versus cost tradeoffs. Blockchain provenance must be verifiable by anyone: link directly to transaction hashes, display smart contract addresses, and surface royalty percentages set by creators. Support multiple blockchain networks but make network selection obvious to prevent users minting on unexpected chains. Collection curation affects discoverability: allow creators to group algorithmic variations while letting collectors filter by generation parameters or visual attributes. Offline-generated art versus on-chain generation represents different trust models — make the distinction clear in presentation. Avoid: gallery views that require vertical scrolling to see more than two artworks, minting interfaces that hide total cost until final confirmation, and any creative submission flow that does not verify creator wallet ownership before publishing.
ui_style_bias: Minimal neutral frame; fast-loading masonry, creator-attributed always, dark-mode gallery default, one-tap minting, and blockchain-transparent provenance

keywords: spatial, vr, ar, vision, os, immersive, mixed-reality, xr, augmented reality, virtual reality, headset, hololens, quest, visionos, passthrough
visual_style: Dimensionally aware and ergonomically grounded. The interface must operate in three spatial axes with depth as the primary organizational principle — information hierarchy is expressed through z-axis positioning, not just visual weight. Typography must remain legible across varying distances and spatial scales, using dynamic scaling that adjusts based on proximity to the user. Glassmorphism and translucency are functional requirements, not aesthetic choices: UI panels must maintain context by allowing the environment to remain visible through interfaces. Interaction feedback must be immediate and spatial — hover states triggered by gaze, tactile confirmation through hand gestures, and audio cues that reinforce spatial positioning. Visual density must be carefully managed: dense UIs cause cognitive overload in 3D space where users cannot selectively ignore background elements as they can on flat screens. The interface should feel anchored to the environment or body-relative depending on task context — persistent utilities follow the user, while content windows remain world-locked. Avoid: 2D UI patterns naively ported to 3D space, opaque panels that obscure environmental awareness, interaction patterns that require prolonged uncomfortable head positions, and interfaces designed without considering depth perception and parallax effects.
landing_page: Hero section must demonstrate spatial capability through embedded interactive 3D preview or video capture showing actual headset POV, not concept renders. Lead with the spatial interaction model: how gaze plus gesture replaces traditional input, how windows exist in space rather than on screens, and how apps integrate with physical environments. Below the fold: supported hardware platforms and input methods, spatial app ecosystem with example use cases showing real implementations, developer SDK and spatial design guidelines prominently featured, and ergonomic comfort commitments addressing eye strain and physical fatigue. Social proof from spatial computing pioneers, enterprise deployments, and accessibility implementations. Technical specifications should clarify field of view, hand tracking accuracy, and passthrough quality without marketing hyperbole. Privacy section must address eye tracking data handling, spatial mapping, and environmental capture permissions. Avoid: hero imagery showing people wearing headsets from third-person view rather than demonstrating first-person spatial experience, feature lists that do not explain how spatial interaction differs from screen-based computing, and marketing that oversells immersion without acknowledging physical comfort limitations.
dashboard_layout: Spatial home as the primary interface: floating windows arranged in the user's field of view with depth-based organization, persistent system controls body-anchored to dominant hand or gaze-following for quick access, and environment-aware layouts that adapt to available physical space. App windows use glassmorphic panels with variable opacity based on content needs — video players and immersive content can go opaque, while productivity apps maintain environmental visibility. Navigation employs progressive disclosure: start with spatial overview showing all active windows, then allow users to focus by bringing windows forward in z-space. Gaze-targeting uses dwell time or pinch confirmation to prevent accidental activation — eyes target, hands confirm. Hand menus appear spatially anchored near the summoning hand to avoid tracking interference. System notifications appear in peripheral vision zones with spatial audio cues directing attention without demanding immediate head movement. Workspace presets allow users to save and restore spatial window arrangements for different contexts. Accessibility features include voice control as alternative to hand gestures, high-contrast modes that maintain glassmorphic depth cues, and reduced motion settings that minimize parallax effects. Avoid: flat window grids that ignore depth axis, opaque system UI that blocks environmental awareness, gaze-only interactions that cause eye fatigue from prolonged targeting, and interface elements placed outside comfortable field of view zones.
color_palette: Translucent frosted glass as the foundational material — UI panels use blur, slight tint, and subtle borders to maintain visibility against varied backgrounds while preserving environmental context. System-wide palette uses neutral grays and whites with carefully controlled opacity to work across diverse real-world environments and lighting conditions. Depth cues come from layering, shadows, and parallax motion rather than aggressive color contrast. Semantic colors for interactive elements follow accessibility standards but appear softer due to glassmorphic treatment: blues for interactive elements, greens for confirmations, ambers for warnings, reds for critical actions and errors. Spatial hierarchy uses color temperature: warmer tones for closer interactive elements, cooler tones for background and ambient information. Text maintains 4.5:1 contrast minimum against glassmorphic backgrounds through dynamic contrast adjustment based on environmental passthrough. Avoid: saturated colors that create visual fatigue in prolonged use, opaque backgrounds that destroy spatial awareness, and color-coding schemes that rely on hue differentiation alone without luminance contrast for accessibility.
essential_ux: Gaze plus gesture is the foundational interaction model, but implementation details determine success or failure. Gaze provides rapid targeting, but pinch or hand confirmation prevents eye-tracking false positives from involuntary eye movements. Implement 230ms hover delay before showing gaze feedback to prevent self-consciousness about natural eye scanning. During active manipulation, ignore gaze entirely and use hand position — users look ahead to target locations while hands lag behind performing the action. Target sizes must be substantially larger than screen-based UI to account for hand-tracking precision limits and spatial depth perception variance. Keep interactive elements within 60-degree horizontal and 40-degree vertical comfortable field of view to prevent neck strain. Content windows should use dynamic scaling: automatically grow slightly as they move farther from the user to maintain apparent size and legibility. Environment awareness is critical: detect surfaces for natural window anchoring, adjust UI opacity when user moves through varied lighting, and warn when physical obstacles approach while user is immersed. Session duration management through ambient cues: gradually increase transparency or suggest breaks after extended periods without forcing interruption. Accessibility cannot be an afterthought in spatial computing — provide voice control, hand-free gaze-blink alternatives, and configurable comfort settings from first launch. Spatial audio must reinforce visual cues without creating audio clutter: use subtle directional sound to guide attention to off-screen notifications. Hand-tracking occlusion and lighting dependency are current platform limitations — design fallback interactions and clear feedback when tracking quality degrades. Avoid: requiring users to hold arms extended for prolonged periods, gaze-only selection without manual confirmation causing accidental activations, placing critical UI outside the comfortable viewing zone, and failing to warn users about physical obstacles during immersive experiences.
ui_style_bias: Glassmorphic depth-first; gaze-pinch confirmed, z-axis hierarchy, dynamic proximity scaling, 60-degree comfort zones, environment-aware translucent panels

keywords: climate, energy, sustainable, green, tech, carbon, renewable, solar, wind, emissions, carbon footprint, impact, environmental, net zero, decarbonization, clean energy
visual_style: Data-forward with restrained visual weight. The interface must balance scientific credibility with approachability — complex environmental data needs to feel trustworthy without intimidating non-technical users. Typography should be clean and technical for data labels, but human and accessible for explanations and contextual guidance. Information density is high by necessity, but must be organized through progressive disclosure: lead with the headline metric or impact score, then allow deeper exploration of methodology and source data. Visualizations should prioritize temporal trends and comparisons over decorative charts — show progress toward targets, historical baselines, and peer benchmarks. The visual language should convey transparency and rigor without clinical coldness. Avoid: greenwashing aesthetics like saturated leaf-greens and nature photography as decoration, oversimplified metrics that obscure methodology, and interfaces that make sustainability feel like optional virtue signaling rather than operational necessity.
landing_page: Hero section establishes impact credibility first: show real measurement in action through an embedded live dashboard excerpt, emissions tracking visualization, or transparent data methodology diagram. Lead with the measurable outcome, not aspirational language. Below the fold: data source integrations and measurement scope coverage, compliance and reporting framework support, methodology transparency section with standards referenced, and impact visualization capabilities. Social proof from recognized environmental organizations, regulatory bodies, or certified B-Corps — not generic testimonials. Pricing must address audit-readiness and reporting compliance as value drivers. Footer should include certification logos and third-party verification badges where applicable. Avoid: green-washed hero imagery with wind turbines or solar panels as decoration, vague claims about carbon neutrality without methodology disclosure, and landing pages that prioritize marketing emotion over measurement transparency.
dashboard_layout: Impact dashboard as the primary view: current emissions or energy metrics with trend direction, progress toward stated reduction targets with projected trajectory, and comparison against baseline or industry benchmarks. Measurement breakdown showing Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions with drilling into contributing sources. Data source integration status with last-sync timestamps and data completeness indicators. Historical trend visualization with annotated intervention points showing cause-effect relationships. Compliance reporting section with pre-formatted exports for CDP, GRI, TCFD, or regulatory frameworks. Scenario modeling for evaluating intervention impact before implementation. Methodology transparency panel explaining calculation methods, data sources, and assumptions. Real-time alerts for threshold breaches or anomalous consumption patterns. Avoid: dashboards that show only top-line metrics without methodology access, visualization-heavy layouts that sacrifice data precision, and interfaces that require manual data entry for core measurements when integrations exist.
color_palette: Restrained earth-tone palette that conveys environmental focus without visual cliché. Use muted natural greens and blues as accents for positive environmental outcomes, never as primary interface color. Warm amber for warnings about targets at risk or efficiency opportunities. Cool grays and soft whites for backgrounds to support high data density without visual fatigue. Data visualizations use colorblind-safe palettes with high contrast — environmental data must be accessible to all stakeholders. Emissions reductions and efficiency gains use directional color coding: declining trend lines in positive green, increasing in warning amber. Avoid decorative gradients or nature-photography color sampling. Carbon intensity and impact metrics should use standardized color scales that remain consistent across the product. Avoid: saturated greens that signal greenwashing, rainbow palettes that confuse semantic meaning, and color choices that prioritize brand expression over data legibility.
essential_ux: Methodology transparency is the trust foundation — every metric must trace back to its calculation method and data sources. Users assume greenwashing until proven otherwise, so design for skepticism by making verification pathways obvious. Data completeness and confidence intervals matter more than precision — show gaps honestly rather than interpolating. Temporal comparisons require careful baseline establishment: migrations between calculation methods or expanded measurement scopes must be annotated clearly to prevent false trend interpretation. Performance optimization is an environmental imperative, not just a UX concern — page weight and rendering efficiency directly contradict climate-positive messaging. Implement aggressive image compression, minimal JavaScript, efficient rendering, and consider carbon-aware hosting. Behavior change requires closing the feedback loop between action and impact: show users how specific interventions moved metrics, not just that metrics changed. Support both operational decision-makers who need rapid answers and auditors who need complete documentation. Offline access for presentations to boards or regulatory bodies. Data export must support both summary reporting and granular analysis. Avoid: interfaces that present impact scores without calculation transparency, and dashboards that treat environmental metrics as vanity KPIs rather than operational drivers.
ui_style_bias: Transparent data-centric; earth-toned restraint, temporal trend focus, methodology-accessible dashboards, Scope 1-2-3 breakdown, and performance-optimized delivery

keywords: smart home, home automation, iot, connected devices, hub, control center, smart hub, home control, automation platform, smart house, device management, scene automation
visual_style: Contextual and device-agnostic. The interface must unify control across manufacturers and protocols into a consistent interaction model that works regardless of device brand or communication standard. Typography should be large and readable at arm's length for wall-mounted tablets or across-room phone usage, with clear labels that use plain language over technical jargon. Layouts prioritize room-based organization over device-type categorization: users think spatially about their homes, not in lists of thermostats and lights. Visual hierarchy emphasizes immediate actions: single-tap controls for frequently used devices prominently displayed, advanced scheduling and automation rules accessible but not cluttering the main view. Status feedback must be instantaneous and unambiguous: when a user taps to turn on a light, visual confirmation appears within 200ms even if the actual device takes longer to respond. The interface should feel ambient and unobtrusive when idle, then responsive and clear during active control. Dark mode and light mode must both be implemented since usage contexts vary from bedside night control to bright kitchen morning routines. Avoid: complex nested menus that require multiple taps to perform basic actions, manufacturer-branded UI inconsistencies between device types, technical error messages when devices fail to respond, and interfaces designed only for phone screens rather than tablets or in-wall panels.
landing_page: Hero section demonstrates unified control through embedded interface preview showing multiple device types controlled from single dashboard, not abstract smart home lifestyle photography. Lead with the interoperability value: supported protocols, device brands, and total compatible devices with live marketplace verification. Below the fold: room-based organization demonstration showing how devices group naturally, automation examples with if-this-then-that visual logic builders, energy monitoring capabilities with real-time consumption tracking, and voice assistant integration options. Security and privacy section addresses local processing versus cloud dependency, encrypted communications, and user data handling. Installation complexity acknowledged honestly: professional setup versus DIY with prerequisite network requirements stated clearly. Social proof from verified installation base and energy savings data, not generic testimonials. Ecosystem expansion path showing how additional devices integrate without reconfiguration. Avoid: hero imagery of isolated smart devices instead of integrated control experience, compatibility claims without specific protocol version support, automation features buried in documentation, and landing pages that oversimplify the technical prerequisites for reliable operation.
dashboard_layout: Home overview as primary interface: spatial floor plan or room grid showing all spaces with device counts and status summaries at a glance, favorite devices pinned at top for single-tap access, and current environmental conditions aggregated across sensors. Room detail views group all devices by physical location with contextual controls: lights show brightness sliders and color pickers, thermostats display current and target temperatures with immediate adjustment, locks show secure-unlocked status with one-tap toggle. Scene triggers prominently displayed: morning routine, leave home, movie time, bedtime with single-tap activation executing multi-device sequences. Automation builder uses visual logic: when-condition-then-action with drag-drop device selection and plain-language rule descriptions. Energy dashboard shows real-time consumption by device and room with historical trends and cost projections. Notification center aggregates alerts: security events prioritized over routine status updates, with configurable quiet hours and device-specific thresholds. Device management panel for adding new devices with protocol auto-detection and guided pairing flows. Family member profiles with permission controls and customized interface layouts. Quick actions accessible from lock screen or notification shade for emergency scenarios. Avoid: flat device lists without spatial organization, automation rules that require scripting knowledge, energy data presented only as raw numbers without context, and notification systems that create alert fatigue through undifferentiated urgency.
color_palette: Adaptive palette that works across lighting conditions. Light mode uses soft backgrounds with high-contrast text for daytime kitchen tablet usage. Dark mode uses deep backgrounds with reduced brightness for bedside night controls. Device status uses intuitive semantic colors: warm amber for active heating, cool blue for active cooling, green for locked and secure, red for alerts and errors. Controllable devices display with higher saturation to indicate interactive state versus read-only sensors shown in muted tones. Energy consumption visualizations use gradient heatmaps from cool efficient to warm inefficient. Room-based color coding optional for visual organization but never required for functional understanding. Accent colors for automation triggers and scenes should be user-customizable to support personal organization systems. Avoid: purely decorative color that adds no functional information, aggressive saturation that causes eye strain during night usage, and color-only status encoding without shape or text redundancy for accessibility.
essential_ux: Device response latency creates trust issues: show optimistic UI updates immediately while background commands execute, but surface timeout errors clearly when devices fail to respond within 3 seconds. Room-based organization must support flexible definitions: users need to create custom zones like outdoor, garage, and basement beyond standard room types. Automation reliability depends on local processing fallback: critical routines like security arming must execute even when internet connectivity fails. Device onboarding is the friction point: implement automatic discovery where possible, provide clear troubleshooting for pairing failures, and never assume users know their WiFi network band or IP address ranges. Energy monitoring provides value only with actionable recommendations: flag phantom loads, identify inefficient devices, and suggest automation rules to reduce consumption. Voice control integration should complement not replace visual interface: some tasks like adjusting multiple light brightnesses are faster with sliders than sequential voice commands. Family member permissions prevent conflicts: kids can control lights but not unlock doors, guests can trigger scenes but not modify automation rules. Notification fatigue is real: default to only security-critical alerts, allow per-device thresholds, and provide routine summaries instead of individual status changes. Cross-protocol communication is invisible to users but critical for reliability: implement device health monitoring, warn when protocols are deprecated, and provide migration paths when manufacturers change cloud dependencies. Session state must persist across devices: starting scene configuration on phone should continue seamlessly on tablet. Avoid: requiring users to know device IP addresses or MAC addresses for troubleshooting, automation interfaces that break when a single device becomes unavailable, energy dashboards that show only current usage without historical baselines for comparison, and setup flows that assume technical expertise with network configuration.
ui_style_bias: Room-spatial organization; instant status feedback, cross-protocol unification, scene-based automation, energy-contextual monitoring, and family-permissioned control
